title: Infection and Immunity
topics: Infectious agents and how they cause disease
Social and psychological effects on patients

notes.h: Infectious agents and how they cause disease
notes.body:
Pathogenicity is whether an organism can cause disease at all; virulence is how much disease it causes, measured for example by the ID50 or LD50. Disease reflects the interaction between microbe and host, so the same organism can be a harmless commensal in one person and a serious pathogen in another. Opportunists such as Pneumocystis jirovecii (advanced HIV) and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (burns) show this clearly.

Main classes of agent
- Bacteria: prokaryotes with 70S ribosomes. Gram-positives have a thick peptidoglycan wall with teichoic acids and stain purple; Gram-negatives have a thin wall plus an outer membrane containing lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and stain pink.
- Viruses: obligate intracellular parasites. Replication runs attachment, entry, uncoating, genome replication and gene expression, assembly and release. HIV gp120 binds CD4 then CCR5 or CXCR4; reverse transcriptase and integrase create a latent reservoir. Influenza A drift (point mutations in HA and NA) drives seasonal epidemics; shift (segment reassortment) can cause pandemics.
- Fungi: eukaryotes with ergosterol in their membranes and glucan/chitin walls (yeasts, moulds, dimorphic fungi).
- Protozoa multiply in the host; most helminths do not, and invasive ones drive eosinophilia and Th2/IgE responses.
- Prions: misfolded PrPSc that templates normal PrPC; resistant to standard sterilisation.

Virulence mechanisms
- Adhesion: P fimbriae of uropathogenic E. coli favour ascending infection to the kidney.
- Evading phagocytosis: capsules (S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, Hib); M. tuberculosis blocks phagolysosome fusion; Listeria escapes the phagosome with listeriolysin O.
- Biofilms on devices tolerate antibiotics, so the device often has to be removed.
- Exotoxins are secreted, potent, mostly heat-labile proteins that can be toxoided. Cholera toxin (AB model): B binds GM1, A ADP-ribosylates Gs-alpha, cAMP rises and CFTR chloride secretion causes watery diarrhoea. Tetanus and botulinum toxins cleave SNAREs: tetanus blocks inhibitory glycine/GABA release (spastic paralysis); botulinum blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction (flaccid paralysis). Superantigens such as TSST-1 link MHC II to the TCR V-beta region and activate huge numbers of T cells.
- Endotoxin (lipid A of LPS) is heat-stable and acts via TLR4 to trigger TNF, IL-1 and IL-6, causing septic shock and DIC.
- P. falciparum PfEMP1 causes cytoadherence and rosetting, so parasitised cells sequester in brain microvessels.
- Transformation, transduction (CTX-phi carries the cholera toxin genes) and conjugation spread virulence genes.

Koch's postulates fail for unculturable organisms, carriers and polymicrobial disease; Falkow's molecular postulates (1988) apply the logic to genes.

Exam pitfalls
- Saying only Gram-negatives make exotoxins.
- Swapping spastic (tetanus) and flaccid (botulism) paralysis.
- Treating virulence as fixed and ignoring host factors such as immunity and colonisation resistance.

Defence is layered: barriers first, then innate responses within minutes to hours, then adaptive responses over days, which leave memory.

Barriers and innate immunity
- Barriers: skin, mucus and cilia, lysozyme, gastric acid, defensins, urine flow, commensals.
- Pattern recognition receptors detect PAMPs: TLR4 (LPS), TLR5 (flagellin), TLR3 (dsRNA), TLR7/8 (ssRNA), TLR9 (CpG DNA). RIG-I senses cytosolic viral RNA and drives type I interferon.
- Complement: classical (C1q on antibody), lectin (MBL on microbial sugars) and alternative (spontaneous C3 hydrolysis) pathways meet at C3 convertase. C3b opsonises, C3a and C5a inflame and recruit, and C5b-9 forms the membrane attack complex. Terminal component deficiency or eculizumab therapy greatly raises the risk of Neisseria infection, so meningococcal vaccination is needed.
- Phagocytes kill using the NADPH oxidase respiratory burst. Chronic granulomatous disease causes catalase-positive infections (S. aureus, Aspergillus) and is screened with the DHR test.
- NK cells kill cells that lack MHC class I ('missing self') with perforin and granzymes, and mediate ADCC through CD16.
- IL-1, IL-6 and TNF cause fever (via PGE2) and acute phase proteins such as CRP.

Adaptive immunity
- MHC I presents cytosolic peptides to CD8 T cells; MHC II presents endocytosed peptides to CD4 T cells.
- Naive T cells need signal 1 (TCR plus peptide-MHC), signal 2 (CD80/86 with CD28) and signal 3 (cytokines such as IL-12). Signal 1 alone tends to cause anergy.
- CD4 subsets: Th1 (IFN-gamma, intracellular pathogens), Th2 (IL-4/5/13, helminths, IgE), Th17 (IL-17, neutrophils), Tfh (B-cell help), Treg (FOXP3, suppression).
- Antibodies neutralise, opsonise, activate complement and drive ADCC. IgM comes first; IgG crosses the placenta; IgA protects mucosae; IgE arms mast cells. Class switching and affinity maturation need Tfh help (CD40L-CD40) and AID; CD40L deficiency causes hyper-IgM syndrome.
- Secondary responses are faster, larger and mainly high-affinity IgG, the basis of boosters.

Vaccination
Active immunity is self-generated and durable; passive immunity (maternal IgG, immunoglobulin) is immediate but fades. Vaccines may be live attenuated, inactivated, toxoid, subunit, conjugate or mRNA. Conjugates turn T-independent polysaccharides into T-dependent antigens, giving memory in infants under 2 and reducing carriage. Live vaccines are generally avoided in severe immunosuppression and pregnancy.

Worked illustration: in influenza, interferon and NK cells limit early spread, IgM appears around day 7 and IgG rises over weeks; re-exposure triggers a rapid memory response.

Evasion includes antigenic variation, protein A, IgA1 proteases and MHC I down-regulation. Sepsis-3 (2016) defines sepsis as life-threatening organ dysfunction (SOFA rise of 2 or more) caused by a dysregulated host response to infection.

Exam pitfalls
- Mixing up MHC I/CD8 and MHC II/CD4.
- Claiming plain polysaccharide vaccines work well in infants.
- Defining sepsis by SIRS criteria rather than organ dysfunction.

Core measures
- Incidence: new cases in a population at risk over a period. Prevalence: the proportion with the disease at a point in time. At steady state, prevalence ≈ incidence × average duration, so treatment that prolongs survival (e.g. antiretrovirals for HIV) raises prevalence even when incidence falls.
- Attack rate = cases ÷ population at risk. Secondary attack rate = cases among contacts ÷ susceptible contacts (leave out immune contacts and the index case).
- Case fatality ratio = deaths ÷ diagnosed cases, inflated if mild cases are missed; mortality rate uses the whole population.

Transmission dynamics
- R0 is the mean number of secondary cases from one case in a fully susceptible population; R0 ≈ β × c × D (transmission probability per contact × contact rate × duration of infectiousness). Re = R0 × s.
- Herd immunity threshold (HIT) = 1 − 1/R0. Critical vaccination coverage Vc = (1 − 1/R0) ÷ E.
- In an SIR epidemic the number infected peaks when s = 1/R0, but infection continues, so the final size overshoots the HIT.
- A latent period shorter than the incubation period allows pre-symptomatic spread. The serial interval is onset-to-onset time; doubling time = ln 2 ÷ r.
- Overdispersion (low k) means a minority of cases cause most transmission.

Worked example: R0 = 6, vaccine effectiveness 0.9. HIT = 1 − 1/6 ≈ 0.83; Vc = 0.83 ÷ 0.9 ≈ 0.93, so about 93% coverage is needed. If E were below 0.83, even 100% coverage could not stop spread.

Diagnostic tests
Sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN); specificity = TN/(TN+FP); PPV = TP/(TP+FP); NPV = TN/(TN+FN). Predictive values depend on prevalence. Screening 1,000 people at 2% prevalence with 90% sensitivity and 95% specificity gives TP = 18 and FP = 49, so PPV = 18/67 ≈ 27%.

Outbreaks and surveillance
- Epidemic curves: point source (one peak spanning about one incubation period), continuing source (plateau), propagated (waves about one serial interval apart).
- Investigation: confirm the outbreak, define and find cases, describe by time, place and person, then test hypotheses (cohort gives relative risk; case-control gives odds ratio) while controlling and communicating.
- Chain of infection: agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, susceptible host. Many emerging infections are zoonoses, hence One Health.
- Surveillance may be passive, active, sentinel or syndromic. In England the Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010 require doctors to notify suspected notifiable diseases without waiting for laboratory confirmation; UKHSA collates the data.

Exam pitfalls
- Confusing efficacy (trials) with effectiveness (real-world use); VE = 1 − RR.
- Forgetting that PPV falls when prevalence is low.
- Including immune contacts in the secondary attack rate denominator.

notes.h: Social and psychological effects on patients
notes.body:
Infection shapes how patients see themselves and are treated, which in turn affects testing, adherence and transmission.

Stigma
- Goffman (1963): stigma is a deeply discrediting attribute that produces a 'spoiled identity'. The discredited have a visible difference; the discreditable must manage disclosure of a concealable condition such as HIV.
- Scambler and Hopkins (1986), studying epilepsy: enacted stigma is actual discrimination; felt stigma is shame and fear of it, which was often more disruptive because it led to concealment.
- HIV stigma delays testing, discourages disclosure, reduces adherence and harms mental health. U = U, supported by PARTNER and PARTNER2, counters it: a person with a sustained undetectable viral load on treatment does not transmit HIV sexually.
- Epidemics breed blame of marginalised groups and an 'infodemic' of misinformation (WHO).

Illness behaviour and health beliefs
- Mechanic (1962): illness behaviour is how people interpret and act on symptoms.
- Parsons' sick role (1951): exemption from duties and blame, in return for wanting to recover and cooperating with competent help; it fits chronic illness poorly.
- Health Belief Model: susceptibility, severity, benefits versus barriers, cues to action, self-efficacy.
- Leventhal's common-sense model: identity, cause, timeline, consequences, cure or control.
- Vaccine hesitancy (WHO SAGE) and the 3Cs: confidence, complacency, convenience. The fraudulent 1998 Wakefield paper, retracted in 2010, was followed by falling MMR uptake and measles outbreaks.

Isolation and quarantine
Brooks et al. (Lancet, 2020) linked quarantine to post-traumatic stress symptoms, confusion and anger, worse with long duration, poor information and financial loss. Stelfox et al. (JAMA, 2003) found isolated inpatients had more gaps in documented care and more preventable adverse events. Isolation should be justified, reviewed and paired with extra contact and support.

Inequality and communication
- Inverse care law (Tudor Hart, 1971): good care is least available where need is greatest. Homelessness, overcrowding, prison and poverty raise TB risk.
- Depression is common in chronic infection and lowers adherence.
- SPIKES (Baile et al., 2000) structures breaking bad news. Concordance means a shared agreement rather than obedience.
- Partner notification: encourage the patient to tell partners or use provider referral. GMC guidance allows disclosure to a known at-risk sexual contact if the patient still refuses, normally telling the patient first and disclosing the minimum.
- Clinicians overestimate demand for antibiotics; explaining the natural course, safety-netting and back-up prescriptions cut use without lowering satisfaction.

Worked illustration: a homeless man with TB who misses doses needs practical support, such as directly observed therapy and housing links, not blame.

Exam pitfalls
- Confusing enacted and felt stigma.
- Presenting the sick role as a good description of chronic illness.
- Treating confidentiality as absolute, or breach as the first step.

Antimicrobials depend on selective toxicity: hitting targets that are absent or different in human cells, such as peptidoglycan, 70S ribosomes, DNA gyrase and bacterial folate synthesis.

Key terms
- Bactericidal (beta-lactams, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones) versus bacteriostatic (tetracyclines, most macrolides). The difference matters most in endocarditis, meningitis and neutropenia.
- MIC: lowest concentration that prevents visible growth; MBC: lowest that kills 99.9%. Breakpoints classify isolates as susceptible or resistant.
- Beta-lactams are time-dependent (fT>MIC); aminoglycosides are concentration-dependent (Cmax/MIC) with a post-antibiotic effect; fluoroquinolones and vancomycin track AUC/MIC.

Mechanisms by target
- Cell wall: beta-lactams bind penicillin-binding proteins and block cross-linking; glycopeptides bind D-Ala-D-Ala and cannot cross the Gram-negative outer membrane.
- Ribosome: aminoglycosides (30S, misreading; oxygen-dependent uptake, so no anaerobic activity); tetracyclines (30S, block tRNA binding); macrolides (50S exit tunnel); linezolid (50S, blocks the initiation complex).
- Nucleic acids: fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; rifampicin inhibits RNA polymerase (rpoB); metronidazole forms DNA-damaging intermediates only in anaerobes and some protozoa.
- Folate: sulfonamides inhibit dihydropteroate synthase and trimethoprim inhibits DHFR, synergistically.
- Membranes: polymyxins bind lipid A; plasmid-mediated mcr-1 resistance was reported in 2015.
- Antivirals: aciclovir needs viral thymidine kinase for activation and then terminates DNA chains; neuraminidase inhibitors stop virion release; antiretrovirals are combined. Antifungals: azoles inhibit 14-alpha-demethylase, polyenes bind ergosterol, echinocandins inhibit glucan synthase. Artemisinins are activated by haem iron.

Resistance
Five mechanisms: enzymatic inactivation (beta-lactamases, ESBLs, carbapenemases such as KPC, OXA-48 and NDM); altered target (PBP2a from mecA in MRSA, D-Ala-D-Lac in VRE, rpoB mutations); reduced permeability (porin loss); efflux; target bypass. Plasmids and other mobile elements spread resistance genes.

Worked example: TB. If resistance mutations arise in about 1 in 10⁶ bacilli for isoniazid and 1 in 10⁸ for rifampicin, a cavity of 10⁸–10⁹ bacilli almost certainly holds mutants resistant to each drug alone, but the chance of one bacillus resisting both is about 1 in 10¹⁴. Combination therapy prevents selection of resistance, and long treatment clears slowly replicating persisters.

Stewardship
UK 'Start Smart – Then Focus': take cultures, start promptly, document the indication, then review at 48–72 hours (stop, switch IV to oral, narrow, continue or outpatient therapy). Clindamycin, cephalosporins, co-amoxiclav and fluoroquinolones carry high C. difficile risk, increased by proton pump inhibitors and age. Synergy underpins E. faecalis endocarditis treatment: amoxicillin with gentamicin or, increasingly, with ceftriaxone, which avoids aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity and still works with high-level aminoglycoside resistance.

Exam pitfalls
- Saying vancomycin covers Gram-negatives.
- Confusing an ESBL (inhibited by clavulanate, carbapenem-susceptible) with a carbapenemase.
- Suggesting rifampicin can be used alone.

cards.b: The organism must be found in every case of the disease, be isolated and grown in pure culture, reproduce the disease when given to a healthy susceptible host, and be recovered again from that host. They fail for unculturable organisms, asymptomatic carriers and diseases caused by several organisms.
Apply the logic to genes rather than whole organisms: the virulence gene should be linked to pathogenic strains, knocking it out should reduce virulence, and restoring it should restore virulence.

Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan wall with teichoic acids that holds crystal violet, so they stain purple. Gram-negative bacteria have a thin peptidoglycan layer plus an outer membrane containing lipopolysaccharide, so they lose the dye and take up the pink counterstain.

Part of the Gram-negative outer membrane. Its lipid A component is sensed by TLR4 (with MD-2 and CD14), driving release of TNF, IL-1 and IL-6. In large amounts this causes fever, vasodilation, capillary leak, DIC and septic shock.

Exotoxins are proteins secreted by Gram-positive or Gram-negative bacteria. They are usually very potent and specific, mostly heat-labile, and can be made into toxoid vaccines. Endotoxin is LPS from the Gram-negative wall: heat-stable, less potent, acts by triggering broad inflammation, and cannot usefully be toxoided.

cards.f: AB toxin model, with cholera toxin as the example
cards.b: The B subunit binds a host receptor (GM1 ganglioside for cholera toxin) and the A subunit is the enzyme. Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates Gs-alpha, which locks adenylate cyclase on. The rise in cAMP drives chloride secretion through CFTR, and water follows, giving profuse watery diarrhoea.

A toxin such as staphylococcal TSST-1 that links MHC class II to the T-cell receptor V-beta region outside the normal peptide groove. This activates a large fraction of all T cells regardless of what antigen they recognise, causing a cytokine storm (toxic shock syndrome).

Both are zinc proteases that cleave SNARE proteins. Tetanospasmin travels back along motor axons to the spinal cord and blocks release of glycine and GABA from inhibitory interneurons, causing spastic paralysis. Botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, causing flaccid paralysis.
Pathogenicity is whether an organism can cause disease at all (a yes/no property). Virulence is how much disease it causes (a matter of degree), measured for example by the ID50 or LD50.
An organism that mainly causes disease when host defences are weakened or barriers are breached. Examples are Pneumocystis jirovecii in advanced HIV and Pseudomonas aeruginosa in burns.

cards.f: Adhesins, with uropathogenic E. coli as the example
cards.b: Surface pili (fimbriae) and proteins that bind specific host receptors so bacteria are not washed away. P fimbriae on uropathogenic E. coli bind glycolipids on urinary tract epithelium, which favours ascending infection to the kidney (pyelonephritis).

A polysaccharide coat that resists phagocytosis and complement deposition. Key encapsulated pathogens are Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae type b, and their capsules are the targets of conjugate vaccines.

A community of microbes held in a self-made extracellular matrix on a surface such as a catheter, prosthetic joint or heart valve. Biofilms tolerate antibiotics and immune attack, so device infections often need the device to be removed.

An infectious misfolded protein (PrPSc) with no nucleic acid. It acts as a template that converts normal host PrPC into the misfolded form, causing a neurodegenerative spongiform encephalopathy such as CJD. Prions resist standard sterilisation, which has consequences for surgical instruments.
Attachment to a host receptor, entry, uncoating, replication of the genome and expression of viral genes, assembly of new virions, and release by budding or cell lysis.

cards.f: How HIV enters and persists in cells
cards.b: gp120 binds CD4 and then a co-receptor (CCR5, or CXCR4 in later disease), and gp41 drives membrane fusion. Reverse transcriptase copies the RNA genome into DNA, and integrase inserts that DNA into the host genome, creating a latent reservoir.

cards.f: Antigenic drift vs antigenic shift (influenza A)
cards.b: Drift is the gradual build-up of point mutations in haemagglutinin and neuraminidase, which causes seasonal epidemics. Shift is reassortment of genome segments between strains (for example from birds or pigs), producing a new subtype to which few people are immune, with pandemic potential.

Eukaryotes whose cell membranes contain ergosterol rather than cholesterol, inside a wall of glucan and chitin. They grow as yeasts (e.g. Candida), moulds (e.g. Aspergillus) or, in dimorphic fungi, as either depending on temperature.

Protozoa are single-celled eukaryotes (e.g. Plasmodium, Giardia, Toxoplasma) that can multiply inside the host. Helminths are multicellular worms. Most do not multiply within the human host, and tissue-invasive ones typically cause eosinophilia and an IgE-rich Th2 response.

cards.f: Why P. falciparum causes severe malaria
cards.b: Infected red cells express PfEMP1 on surface knobs, which makes them stick to endothelium (e.g. ICAM-1, CD36) and to uninfected red cells (rosetting). Parasitised cells therefore collect in the microvasculature of the brain and other organs, avoid clearance by the spleen and cause cerebral malaria and organ failure.

cards.f: Three routes of horizontal gene transfer in bacteria
cards.b: Transformation is uptake of free DNA. Transduction is transfer by a bacteriophage: the cholera toxin genes, for example, are carried by the phage CTX-phi. Conjugation is transfer of plasmids through direct cell-to-cell contact.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis stops the phagosome maturing and fusing with lysosomes, so it survives inside macrophages. Listeria monocytogenes uses listeriolysin O to escape the phagosome into the cytosol, then spreads from cell to cell by actin polymerisation.

cards.f: Colonisation resistance by the normal microbiota
cards.b: Resident microbes compete with pathogens for nutrients and attachment sites and produce inhibitory substances. Broad-spectrum antibiotics disturb this balance, allowing overgrowth of organisms such as Clostridioides difficile or Candida.

Innate immunity is present from birth, acts within minutes to hours and recognises conserved microbial patterns, but has little memory. Adaptive immunity (T and B cells) takes days to develop, is highly specific because of rearranged receptors, and leaves immunological memory.

cards.f: Physical and chemical barriers to infection
cards.b: Intact skin and its low pH, mucus and ciliary clearance in the airways, lysozyme in tears and saliva, gastric acid, antimicrobial peptides such as defensins, and flushing by urine flow. Commensal flora add colonisation resistance.

PAMPs are conserved microbial molecules recognised by PRRs. Examples: TLR4 senses LPS, TLR5 flagellin, TLR3 double-stranded RNA, TLR7/8 single-stranded RNA and TLR9 unmethylated CpG DNA. Cytosolic sensors such as RIG-I detect viral RNA and drive type I interferon.

Classical pathway: C1q binds antibody on antigen. Lectin pathway: mannose-binding lectin binds microbial sugars. Alternative pathway: spontaneous C3 hydrolysis, amplified on microbial surfaces. All three meet at C3 convertase.

C3b opsonises microbes for phagocytosis. C3a and C5a are anaphylatoxins that cause inflammation and recruit cells. C5b-9 forms the membrane attack complex, which lyses some organisms, especially Neisseria. Complement also clears immune complexes.

cards.f: Terminal complement (C5-C9) deficiency or eculizumab therapy
cards.b: Both cause loss of membrane attack complex activity and a greatly increased risk of recurrent or severe Neisseria meningitidis infection. Patients starting eculizumab therefore need meningococcal vaccination.

An inherited defect in phagocyte NADPH oxidase, so there is no respiratory burst. Patients get recurrent infections and granulomas with catalase-positive organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus. Screening uses the dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry test.

Innate lymphocytes that kill virus-infected and tumour cells which have reduced MHC class I ('missing self'). They kill using perforin and granzymes, perform ADCC through CD16 (an Fc receptor) and secrete IFN-gamma.

cards.f: MHC class I vs class II
cards.b: Class I is on all nucleated cells and presents peptides from inside the cell (cytosolic, e.g. viral) to CD8 T cells. Class II is on professional antigen-presenting cells and presents peptides from outside the cell, taken in by endocytosis, to CD4 T cells.

cards.f: Three signals for activating a naive T cell
cards.b: Signal 1: the TCR recognises a peptide-MHC complex. Signal 2: co-stimulation, e.g. CD80/86 on the dendritic cell binding CD28. Signal 3: polarising cytokines such as IL-12. Signal 1 without signal 2 tends to cause anergy (unresponsiveness).

Th1 (IFN-gamma) activates macrophages against intracellular pathogens. Th2 (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13) acts against helminths and drives IgE. Th17 (IL-17) recruits neutrophils against extracellular bacteria and fungi. Tfh helps B cells in germinal centres. Treg (FOXP3, IL-10, TGF-beta) suppresses responses.

IgM: the first produced, a pentamer, a strong complement activator. IgG: most abundant in serum and crosses the placenta. IgA: a dimer secreted at mucosal surfaces. IgE: binds mast cells, important in helminth defence and allergy. IgD: found with IgM on naive B cells.

Both happen in germinal centres and depend on T-follicular-helper cells (CD40L binding CD40, plus cytokines) and on the enzyme AID. Somatic hypermutation followed by selection produces higher-affinity antibodies. CD40L deficiency causes hyper-IgM syndrome.

The primary response has a lag of about 1-2 weeks and is mainly IgM. The secondary response, from memory B cells, is faster and larger, and mainly high-affinity IgG (or IgA or IgE). This is the basis of booster vaccination.

Neutralisation (blocking toxins or microbial attachment), opsonisation for phagocytosis through Fc receptors, complement activation by the classical pathway, and antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity by NK cells.

Active immunity is produced by the host's own immune response to infection or vaccination and is long-lasting. Passive immunity is pre-formed antibody, either maternal IgG across the placenta or in breast milk, or given as immunoglobulin. It works at once but fades within weeks to months.

Live attenuated (MMR, BCG, oral rotavirus), inactivated whole organism (e.g. inactivated polio), toxoid (tetanus, diphtheria), subunit or recombinant (hepatitis B, HPV), conjugate (Hib, pneumococcal, MenACWY) and mRNA. Live vaccines are generally contraindicated in severe immunosuppression and pregnancy.

cards.f: Why conjugate vaccines work in infants
cards.b: Pure polysaccharides are T-independent antigens: they give poor responses under about 2 years of age and little memory. Linking the polysaccharide to a protein carrier lets B cells present carrier peptides to helper T cells, which drives class switching, affinity maturation, memory and a reduction in nasopharyngeal carriage.

Rubor (redness), calor (heat), tumor (swelling), dolor (pain) and functio laesa (loss of function). They result from vasodilation, increased vascular permeability and mediators such as histamine, prostaglandins, bradykinin and cytokines.

IL-6 (with IL-1 and TNF) causes the liver to make acute phase proteins such as CRP, which opsonises bacteria and activates complement. The same cytokines raise the hypothalamic set-point through prostaglandin E2, causing fever.

Antigenic variation (trypanosome surface glycoprotein, gonococcal pili). Staphylococcal protein A binds the Fc of IgG. IgA1 proteases (Neisseria, Haemophilus). Herpesviruses and HIV down-regulate MHC class I. Capsules block complement deposition.

Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection, with organ dysfunction defined as a rise in SOFA score of 2 points or more. Septic shock adds persistent hypotension needing vasopressors to keep MAP at 65 mmHg or above and a lactate above 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation.

Incidence is the number of new cases in a population at risk over a set period. Prevalence is the proportion of the population with the disease at a given time. In a steady state with low prevalence, prevalence is roughly incidence multiplied by average disease duration.

cards.f: Attack rate and secondary attack rate
cards.b: Attack rate = cases / population at risk during an outbreak, usually given as a percentage. Secondary attack rate = cases among contacts of index cases / number of susceptible contacts, a measure of how easily infection spreads between people.
The average number of secondary cases produced by one infectious person in a completely susceptible population. If R0 is above 1 an epidemic can grow; below 1 it dies out.

R0 is roughly beta x c x D: the probability of transmission per contact, times the contact rate, times the duration of infectiousness. Interventions act on these: masks and vaccines reduce beta, distancing reduces c, and isolation or treatment shortens D.

The average number of secondary cases per case at a given time, allowing for immunity and control measures. In a simple homogeneous model Re = R0 x s, where s is the proportion of the population still susceptible.
HIT = 1 - 1/R0, the proportion of the population that must be immune for Re to fall below 1. Measles (R0 about 12-18) needs above 90%. An infection with R0 = 4 needs 75%.
Vc = (1 - 1/R0) / E, where E is vaccine effectiveness against transmission. If E is less than the herd immunity threshold, elimination by vaccination alone is impossible even at 100% coverage.
VE = (ARU - ARV) / ARU = 1 - RR, where ARU and ARV are the attack rates in unvaccinated and vaccinated people. Efficacy is measured in trials; effectiveness is measured in real-world use.

Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN): the proportion of people with the disease who test positive. Specificity = TN / (TN + FP): the proportion of people without the disease who test negative. Both are properties of the test and change little with prevalence.
PPV = TP / (TP + FP) and NPV = TN / (TN + FN). These depend strongly on prevalence: in low-prevalence settings even a highly specific test gives many false positives, so PPV falls.

Incubation period runs from infection to symptom onset; latent period runs from infection to the start of infectiousness. If the latent period is shorter than the incubation period, people can transmit before symptoms appear, which makes isolating symptomatic cases less effective.

The time between symptom onset in a primary case and symptom onset in the person they infect. With growth rate r and serial interval, R can be estimated from early epidemic data. Doubling time = ln 2 / r.

Point source: one sharp peak spanning about one incubation period. Continuing common source: a plateau. Propagated (person-to-person): a series of increasingly tall waves about one serial interval apart.

cards.f: Case fatality ratio vs mortality rate
cards.b: Case fatality ratio = deaths from the disease / diagnosed cases, a measure of severity. Mortality rate = deaths / total population over a period. CFR is inflated when mild cases go undiagnosed.
Infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, and a susceptible host. Control measures aim to break one or more links.
Direct and indirect contact, respiratory droplets and aerosols (airborne), faecal-oral, vector-borne, blood-borne or sexual, and vertical (mother to child).

An infection naturally transmitted from vertebrate animals to humans, e.g. rabies, brucellosis, avian influenza and Q fever. Many emerging infections are zoonotic, which is the rationale for a One Health approach.

Under the Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010, registered medical practitioners must notify the proper officer of the local authority when they suspect a notifiable disease, without waiting for laboratory confirmation. UKHSA collates the data for surveillance.

cards.f: Relative risk vs odds ratio in outbreak studies
cards.b: In a retrospective cohort (e.g. everyone at a wedding), compare attack rates in exposed and unexposed people to get the relative risk. When the population is not well defined, a case-control study compares odds of exposure in cases and controls to give an odds ratio, which approximates RR when the disease is rare.

Confirm the diagnosis and that there is an outbreak, write a case definition, find cases, describe them by time, place and person, form hypotheses, test them analytically, put control measures in place (often from the start) and communicate the findings.

Divides the population into Susceptible, Infectious and Recovered compartments. The number of people currently infected peaks when the susceptible fraction falls to 1/R0 (Re = 1); new infections continue past this point, so the final epidemic size overshoots the herd immunity threshold.

Passive: routine reports, e.g. notifications, which are cheap but under-report. Active: investigators actively look for cases. Sentinel: selected practices or labs report in detail, e.g. GP influenza-like illness. Syndromic: monitors symptom patterns or calls to NHS 111.

Secondary cases are often very unevenly distributed: a minority of cases cause most transmission. This is captured by the dispersion parameter k, where low k means more superspreading, as with SARS. It makes targeting high-risk settings efficient and lets many introductions die out by chance.

Stigma is an attribute that is deeply discrediting and reduces a person to a 'spoiled identity'. Goffman separated the discredited, whose difference is visible or known, from the discreditable, who have a concealable condition and must manage disclosure.

cards.f: Enacted vs felt stigma (Scambler and Hopkins, 1986)
cards.b: Enacted stigma is actual discrimination. Felt stigma is the shame and fear of discrimination. In their study of epilepsy, felt stigma was more disruptive than enacted stigma because it led people to conceal their condition and withdraw.

cards.f: Effects of HIV stigma on health
cards.b: Fear of stigma delays testing and diagnosis, discourages disclosure to partners and services, and reduces engagement and adherence to antiretroviral therapy. It also harms mental health.

A person living with HIV on effective antiretroviral therapy with a sustained undetectable viral load does not pass HIV on through sex. This is supported by the PARTNER and PARTNER2 studies. It is a powerful message against stigma and an incentive to stay in care.

cards.f: Psychological effects of quarantine (Brooks et al., Lancet 2020 review)
cards.b: A rapid review found frequent post-traumatic stress symptoms, confusion and anger. Longer duration, fear of infection, frustration, boredom, poor supplies, poor information and financial loss made things worse. Clear communication and keeping quarantine as short as possible helped.

cards.f: Harms of contact isolation in hospital
cards.b: Stelfox et al. (JAMA, 2003) found isolated patients had more gaps in documented care (vital signs not recorded, days without physician notes), more preventable adverse events and more complaints. Observational studies also show clinicians enter isolation rooms less often. Other work links isolation to more anxiety and depression. Isolation should therefore be justified, reviewed and paired with extra support.

The different ways people notice, interpret and act on symptoms, including whether and when they seek help. It is shaped by culture, knowledge, how visible and serious the symptoms are, how they disrupt daily life, and access to care.

Rights: exemption from normal social duties and not being blamed for the illness. Obligations: wanting to get well, and seeking and cooperating with technically competent help. The model fits acute illness but fits chronic or stigmatised conditions poorly.

Health behaviour depends on perceived susceptibility, perceived severity, perceived benefits weighed against perceived barriers, cues to action and self-efficacy. It is often used to explain take-up of vaccination and screening.

Hesitancy is a delay in accepting, or refusal of, vaccines despite services being available (WHO SAGE). The 3Cs model names confidence (trust), complacency (low perceived risk) and convenience (access). WHO listed hesitancy among ten threats to global health in 2019.

A 1998 Lancet paper suggesting a link between MMR, bowel disease and autism. It was found to be fraudulent and was retracted in 2010, and Wakefield was struck off. Large studies show no link, but falling MMR uptake was followed by measles outbreaks.

Good medical care tends to be least available to the populations that need it most. In infection this is seen in higher TB, HIV and COVID-19 burdens in deprived groups, alongside poorer access to testing and treatment.

Overcrowded housing, homelessness, poverty, insecure work with no sick pay, imprisonment, migration from high-incidence countries and substance use all increase exposure, susceptibility or delays to diagnosis. TB is the classic example.

Patients build their own picture of an illness along five dimensions: identity (label and symptoms), cause, timeline, consequences, and whether it can be cured or controlled. These beliefs, plus emotional responses, drive coping and adherence.

cards.f: SPIKES protocol for breaking bad news
cards.b: Setting, Perception (what the patient already understands), Invitation (how much they want to know), Knowledge (giving information in small chunks), Emotions (responding with empathy) and Strategy and Summary. From Baile et al., 2000.

Clinicians should first encourage the patient to inform at-risk partners or use anonymous provider referral. GMC guidance allows disclosure to a known sexual contact at risk of a serious communicable disease if the patient still refuses. The patient should normally be told beforehand, and only the minimum necessary should be disclosed.

Depression is more common in people living with HIV and other chronic infections. It worsens quality of life and reduces adherence and engagement with care, so screening and treating mental health is part of infection management.

Signs and symptoms that develop during or after an infection consistent with COVID-19, continue for more than 12 weeks and are not explained by another diagnosis. Fatigue, breathlessness and cognitive problems are common and affect work and identity.

WHO's term for an overload of information, including false or misleading information, during an epidemic. It causes confusion, risky behaviour and mistrust of health authorities and undermines the response.

Compliance implies the patient obeys the prescriber. Adherence is how far behaviour matches the agreed recommendations. Concordance stresses a shared agreement reached between patient and clinician. Poor adherence to antimicrobials risks treatment failure and resistance.

Clinicians often overestimate how much patients expect antibiotics, and perceived pressure drives unnecessary prescribing for self-limiting respiratory infections. Explaining the natural course of the illness, safety-netting and delayed (back-up) prescriptions reduce use without lowering satisfaction.

Epidemics are often blamed on marginalised groups, as in the early AIDS epidemic or anti-Asian harassment during COVID-19. This leads to discrimination, discourages testing and diverts attention from how the infection actually spreads.

An antimicrobial should harm the microbe at concentrations that are safe for the host, by hitting targets that are absent or different in human cells. Examples: peptidoglycan synthesis, bacterial 70S ribosomes, DNA gyrase and bacterial folate synthesis.

Bactericidal drugs kill bacteria (e.g. beta-lactams, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones). Bacteriostatic drugs stop growth so host defences can clear the infection (e.g. tetracyclines, most macrolides). The difference matters most in endocarditis, meningitis and neutropenia.

The lowest drug concentration that prevents visible growth of an organism in vitro under standard conditions. Breakpoints compare the MIC with achievable drug levels to report an isolate as susceptible or resistant. The minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) is the lowest concentration that kills 99.9% of the inoculum.

Penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems and monobactams bind penicillin-binding proteins (transpeptidases) and block peptidoglycan cross-linking. The wall weakens and autolysins are released, causing lysis of growing bacteria.

Bind the D-Ala-D-Ala end of peptidoglycan precursors and block their incorporation into the wall. They are too large to cross the Gram-negative outer membrane, so they work only against Gram-positives. Vancomycin-resistant enterococci change the target to D-Ala-D-Lac.

Beta-lactamases hydrolyse the beta-lactam ring. Inhibitors such as clavulanic acid, tazobactam and avibactam protect partner drugs (e.g. co-amoxiclav). Extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBLs) hydrolyse third-generation cephalosporins, and carbapenemases (KPC, OXA-48, NDM) also hydrolyse carbapenems.
The mecA gene, carried on the mobile SCCmec element, encodes PBP2a. This transpeptidase has low affinity for almost all beta-lactams, so wall synthesis continues in their presence.

Bind the 30S ribosomal subunit and cause misreading of mRNA, which is rapidly bactericidal and concentration-dependent. Uptake needs oxygen-dependent transport, so they do not work against anaerobes. Main toxicities are to the kidney and the ear (ototoxicity).

Tetracyclines bind the 30S subunit and block aminoacyl-tRNA from binding the A site. Macrolides (e.g. clarithromycin) bind the 50S subunit in the exit tunnel and block elongation and translocation. Both are generally bacteriostatic and cover atypical organisms such as Mycoplasma.

Binds the 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit and prevents assembly of the 70S initiation complex. It is active against Gram-positives including MRSA and VRE. Prolonged use can cause myelosuppression and neuropathy.

Inhibit DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV, causing double-strand DNA breaks and cell death. Resistance arises through mutations in gyrA/parC and through efflux. They are associated with C. difficile infection and with tendon and other adverse effects.

These block two successive steps in bacterial folate synthesis. Sulfonamides are PABA analogues that inhibit dihydropteroate synthase; trimethoprim inhibits bacterial dihydrofolate reductase. Humans get folate from their diet, which gives selectivity. Combined, they act synergistically (co-trimoxazole).

Inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (encoded by rpoB). Resistance from single rpoB mutations emerges quickly if it is used alone, so it is always combined in TB. It is a strong liver enzyme inducer with many drug interactions and turns body fluids orange.

A prodrug reduced only in anaerobic bacteria and some protozoa (e.g. Giardia, Trichomonas, Entamoeba) into reactive intermediates that damage DNA. This explains its selective activity against anaerobes.

For beta-lactams, efficacy depends on the time free drug stays above the MIC (fT>MIC). For aminoglycosides it depends on peak concentration relative to MIC (Cmax/MIC), helped by a post-antibiotic effect. For fluoroquinolones and vancomycin, AUC/MIC is the usual target.

cards.f: Five main mechanisms of antimicrobial resistance
cards.b: Enzymatic inactivation (e.g. beta-lactamases), altered target (e.g. PBP2a, rpoB mutations), reduced permeability (porin loss), active efflux pumps, and bypass of the target pathway (e.g. an alternative DHFR).

A guanosine analogue first phosphorylated by viral (HSV/VZV) thymidine kinase, then by host kinases, to the triphosphate. This inhibits viral DNA polymerase and causes chain termination. Activation needs the viral enzyme, which gives selectivity. Resistance usually involves thymidine kinase mutations.

Block influenza neuraminidase, which normally cleaves sialic acid to release new virions from the infected cell. Virus stays attached to the cell surface and spread is limited. They work best when started early in illness.

Nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors, non-nucleoside RT inhibitors, integrase strand-transfer inhibitors, protease inhibitors and entry inhibitors (e.g. the CCR5 antagonist maraviroc). They are used in combination to suppress replication fully and prevent resistance.

Azoles inhibit lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase (ergosterol synthesis) and also inhibit human CYP450 enzymes. Polyenes (amphotericin B, nystatin) bind ergosterol and form membrane pores. Echinocandins inhibit beta-(1,3)-D-glucan synthase in the cell wall.

cards.f: Antimicrobial stewardship: Start Smart - Then Focus
cards.b: UK guidance: start effective treatment promptly after taking cultures, document the indication, then review at 48-72 hours. At review the decision is to stop, switch IV to oral, change or narrow, continue, or arrange outpatient therapy. The aim is to preserve antimicrobial effectiveness and reduce harms such as C. difficile infection.

cards.f: Antibiotics with high C. difficile risk
cards.b: Broad-spectrum agents that disrupt the colonic microbiota, classically clindamycin, cephalosporins (especially later generations), co-amoxiclav and fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin. Proton pump inhibitors and older age add to the risk.

Damage to the cell wall from a beta-lactam or glycopeptide increases aminoglycoside entry into enterococci and streptococci. Together they kill bacteria that each drug alone only inhibits, which is the classic rationale in enterococcal endocarditis. High-level aminoglycoside resistance removes the synergy. For E. faecalis endocarditis, amoxicillin plus ceftriaxone is increasingly used instead of amoxicillin plus gentamicin: it avoids aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity and still works when there is high-level aminoglycoside resistance.

Artemisinin derivatives have an endoperoxide bridge that is activated by haem iron inside the parasite, producing free radicals that damage parasite proteins. They clear parasites very fast and are given as artemisinin-based combination therapy to protect against resistance.

Cationic peptides that bind lipid A of LPS, displace stabilising divalent cations and disrupt the Gram-negative outer and inner membranes. They are a last-resort option for some carbapenem-resistant Gram-negatives but are nephrotoxic. Plasmid-mediated resistance (mcr-1) was reported in 2015.

questions.q: Which structure is found in Gram-negative bacteria but not in Gram-positive bacteria?
options: An outer membrane containing lipopolysaccharide
A thick peptidoglycan layer containing teichoic acids
A cytoplasmic membrane made of a phospholipid bilayer
70S ribosomes
questions.why: Only Gram-negative bacteria have an outer membrane, and its outer leaflet contains LPS (endotoxin). All bacteria have a cytoplasmic membrane and 70S ribosomes, and a thick teichoic-acid-rich wall is the Gram-positive feature.

questions.q: A 58-year-old gardener comes in 10 days after a deep puncture wound from a rose thorn. He has jaw stiffness (trismus) and painful generalised muscle spasms, and his vaccination history is unknown. How does the toxin responsible cause these features?
options: It blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction
It blocks release of glycine and GABA from inhibitory spinal interneurons
It ADP-ribosylates elongation factor 2 and stops protein synthesis
It cross-links MHC class II and T-cell receptors and causes a cytokine storm
questions.why: Tetanospasmin travels back along motor axons and cleaves synaptobrevin in inhibitory interneurons, which removes inhibition of motor neurons and causes spastic paralysis. Blocking acetylcholine release is how botulinum toxin works, and inhibiting EF-2 is how diphtheria toxin works.

questions.q: Which toxin is correctly matched with its mechanism?
options: Diphtheria toxin: acts as a superantigen by binding T-cell receptor V-beta
TSST-1: cleaves SNARE proteins at the neuromuscular junction
Cholera toxin: ADP-ribosylates Gs-alpha, which keeps adenylate cyclase active
Shiga toxin: ADP-ribosylates Gi-alpha in enterocytes
questions.why: Cholera toxin keeps Gs active, so cAMP rises and chloride secretion through CFTR drives watery diarrhoea. Diphtheria toxin inactivates EF-2, TSST-1 is the superantigen, and Shiga toxin removes an adenine from 28S rRNA in the 60S ribosomal subunit, stopping protein synthesis.

questions.q: Compare bacterial exotoxins and endotoxin, giving four differences.
markScheme: Exotoxins are proteins secreted by Gram-positive or Gram-negative bacteria; endotoxin is the lipid A of LPS in the Gram-negative outer membrane
Exotoxins are highly potent and act on specific targets; endotoxin acts less specifically by triggering inflammation through TLR4
Exotoxins are mostly heat-labile; endotoxin is heat-stable
Exotoxins can be made into toxoids for vaccines (e.g. tetanus, diphtheria); endotoxin is a poor immunogen and is not used for toxoids
questions.modelAnswer: Exotoxins are proteins actively released by both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. Endotoxin is the lipid A part of lipopolysaccharide, an integral part of the Gram-negative outer membrane that is released mainly when cells lyse. Exotoxins are extremely potent and act on specific targets, as with tetanospasmin and cholera toxin. Endotoxin causes broad inflammation through TLR4, leading to fever and shock. Most exotoxins are destroyed by heat, whereas endotoxin is heat-stable. Exotoxins can be inactivated to make protective toxoid vaccines, but endotoxin cannot be used this way.

questions.q: Explain how influenza A virus causes both annual seasonal epidemics and occasional pandemics.
markScheme: Influenza A has a segmented RNA genome and an error-prone RNA polymerase with no proofreading
Antigenic drift: point mutations accumulate in haemagglutinin and neuraminidase and partly evade existing antibodies, causing seasonal epidemics and the need to update vaccines every year
Antigenic shift: two strains infecting the same cell (often an animal host such as a pig) exchange genome segments, producing a new HA and/or NA subtype
Few people are immune to a shifted subtype, so it can spread worldwide as a pandemic (e.g. 1957, 1968, and the 2009 H1N1 reassortant)
questions.modelAnswer: Influenza A has eight RNA genome segments and an RNA polymerase that cannot proofread. Copying errors build up in the antigenic sites of haemagglutinin and neuraminidase, so neutralising antibodies from earlier infection or vaccination bind less well. This antigenic drift lets the virus reinfect people every winter, which is why vaccine strains are reviewed each year. Occasionally two different viruses, for example an avian and a human strain, infect the same cell, often in a pig, and swap segments. This antigenic shift produces a virus with a new HA or NA to which most people have no immunity, and a pandemic may follow, as in 2009.

questions.q: Koch's postulates are a cornerstone of microbiology. Explain three reasons why they cannot always be satisfied, and describe how molecular approaches have addressed these limitations.
markScheme: Some organisms cannot be grown in pure culture (e.g. Treponema pallidum, Mycobacterium leprae)
Asymptomatic carriage (e.g. meningococcus, polio, Salmonella Typhi) breaks the rule that the organism appears only in disease
Some diseases are polymicrobial, depend on host factors, or have no ethical or suitable animal model to show causation
Falkow's molecular Koch's postulates link specific virulence genes to disease by knocking them out and restoring them
Nucleic acid detection and sequencing (PCR, metagenomics) identify unculturable organisms and establish causal links, e.g. Tropheryma whipplei
questions.modelAnswer: The postulates require pure culture, but Treponema pallidum and Mycobacterium leprae cannot be grown on artificial media. They assume the organism is absent in health, yet many pathogens are carried asymptomatically, such as Neisseria meningitidis in the nasopharynx. Some diseases need several organisms or particular host susceptibility, and for human-specific pathogens deliberately infecting a healthy host is unethical or no animal model exists. Falkow's molecular postulates move the focus to virulence genes: a gene should be linked to pathogenic strains, its inactivation should reduce virulence and restoring it should bring virulence back. Sequence-based methods such as PCR and metagenomics identified unculturable agents like Tropheryma whipplei, allowing causation to be inferred without culture.

questions.q:
A 19-year-old first-year student is brought to the emergency department 14 hours after developing fever, headache and leg pain. She now has a spreading purpuric, non-blanching rash. Her temperature is 39.4 C, pulse 132/min, blood pressure 84/46 mmHg, capillary refill time 5 seconds and lactate 5.1 mmol/L. Blood cultures later grow Gram-negative diplococci, confirmed as Neisseria meningitidis serogroup B. Her flatmate is well but is found to carry the same organism in her throat.

Explain the pathogenesis of this infection, from colonisation to the clinical picture described. Include why her flatmate is well, and why adolescents and young adults are a group at particular risk.
markScheme: Transmission by respiratory droplets or close contact; colonisation of nasopharyngeal mucosa using type IV pili and outer-membrane adhesins
IgA1 protease and antigenic or phase variation of surface proteins help it persist on the mucosa
Crossing the epithelium into the blood; the polysaccharide capsule (and sialylation, factor H binding) resists complement and phagocytosis
Lipooligosaccharide (endotoxin) and outer-membrane blebs strongly activate TLR4, releasing TNF, IL-1 and IL-6
Endothelial damage, capillary leak, vasodilation and DIC explain the purpura, hypotension, poor perfusion and raised lactate (septic shock)
Carriage without disease depends on host immunity (bactericidal antibody, intact complement) and on strain virulence, so asymptomatic carriage is common
Adolescents and young adults have high carriage and close-contact social mixing (halls, parties, shared drinks), and antibody from childhood exposure may have waned
Link to defences: terminal complement deficiency predisposes; conjugate MenACWY and MenB vaccines target capsule or protein antigens
Answer clearly structured from entry to disease, with accurate interpretation of the observations
questions.modelAnswer:
N. meningitidis is a strictly human organism spread by respiratory droplets and close contact. It attaches to non-ciliated nasopharyngeal epithelium using type IV pili, then binds more tightly through outer-membrane proteins such as Opa and Opc. On the mucosa it survives by cleaving secretory IgA1 with IgA1 protease and by switching its surface antigens on and off (phase and antigenic variation).

In most people this is the end of the story: carriage. Up to about a quarter of older teenagers carry meningococci at any one time, and serum bactericidal antibodies plus an intact complement system stop invasion. The flatmate shows this. Disease happens when a virulent strain meets a host without bactericidal antibody against it, sometimes helped by damage to the mucosa from viral infection or smoking.

Invasive bacteria cross the epithelium and enter the bloodstream. The polysaccharide capsule, sialylation of lipooligosaccharide (LOS) and recruitment of the host regulator factor H all reduce deposition of C3b and the membrane attack complex, so the organism multiplies rapidly. It sheds outer-membrane blebs packed with LOS, a potent TLR4 agonist, and the resulting surge of TNF, IL-1 and IL-6 activates endothelium and coagulation. This causes vasodilation, capillary leak, microthrombosis and consumption of clotting factors (DIC). These processes explain the findings: purpura from haemorrhage into the skin and vessel thrombosis, hypotension and tachycardia from vasodilation and fluid loss into tissues, slow capillary refill, and lactate of 5.1 from tissue hypoperfusion. This is septic shock. Bacteria can also cross the blood-brain barrier and cause meningitis.

Adolescents and young adults have a second peak of disease because carriage is highest in this group, they mix closely (shared halls, kissing, crowded social events), and the antibody they developed in childhood may have waned. Complement studies explain the role of the membrane attack complex: people lacking C5-C9, or taking eculizumab, have greatly increased risk. Prevention therefore targets both carriage and invasion. The MenACWY conjugate vaccine for teenagers reduces carriage of the capsular groups it covers. Serogroup B capsule resembles host neural sugars and is poorly immunogenic, so MenB vaccines are built from outer-membrane proteins instead.

questions.q:
Following flooding, cholera breaks out in a displacement camp of 20,000 people. Over three weeks, 600 people develop acute watery diarrhoea, some losing litres of 'rice-water' stool a day, and 12 die. Stool culture grows Vibrio cholerae O1. Most cases have drunk untreated water from one river collection point. Health workers report that oral rehydration solution (ORS) containing glucose and sodium works remarkably well, even though the diarrhoea continues.

(a) Calculate the attack rate and case fatality ratio. (b) Explain the molecular pathogenesis of cholera, including how the toxin genes are acquired and how the toxin produces secretory diarrhoea. (c) Explain why glucose-sodium ORS works in cholera. (d) Comment on why V. cholerae needs a relatively large infecting dose and what this implies for control.
markScheme: Faecal-oral spread via contaminated water; the organism must survive gastric acid, which is why the infectious dose is high (relevant to antacid use and achlorhydria)
Motility (flagellum) and mucinase let it reach the epithelium; toxin-coregulated pilus (TCP) is needed for colonisation of the small intestine
ctxAB genes are carried by the filamentous bacteriophage CTX-phi, which uses TCP as its receptor: an example of horizontal gene transfer (transduction/lysogenic conversion)
B pentamer binds GM1 ganglioside; the A subunit ADP-ribosylates Gs-alpha, so adenylate cyclase stays permanently active
Raised cAMP activates protein kinase A, which opens CFTR chloride channels and inhibits NaCl absorption; water follows, and the mucosa is not invaded or inflamed
SGLT1 sodium-glucose co-transport is unaffected by cAMP, so glucose drives sodium and therefore water absorption despite ongoing secretion
Death results from hypovolaemic shock and electrolyte loss; rehydration alone lowers the CFR greatly
Control: safe water, sanitation, hygiene, oral cholera vaccine, case management and surveillance
Clear structure with calculations shown and mechanisms linked to clinical features
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The attack rate is 600/20,000 = 3% over three weeks, and the case fatality ratio is 12/600 = 2%. With good rehydration the CFR should fall below 1%, so 2% suggests late presentation or limited access to treatment.

(b) V. cholerae is spread by the faecal-oral route, here clearly through contaminated river water. It is acid-sensitive, so most ingested organisms die in the stomach. Survivors use their single polar flagellum and mucinase to cross the mucus layer of the small intestine and colonise the epithelium using the toxin-coregulated pilus (TCP). The organism does not invade.

The ctxA and ctxB toxin genes are not part of the core vibrio chromosome. They are carried by the filamentous bacteriophage CTX-phi, which infects V. cholerae through TCP and integrates into the chromosome (lysogenic conversion). This shows how horizontal gene transfer can turn a harmless environmental vibrio into a pathogen.

Cholera toxin is an AB5 toxin. The B pentamer binds GM1 ganglioside on enterocytes, and the A1 fragment reaches the cytosol, where it ADP-ribosylates Gs-alpha and blocks its GTPase activity. Adenylate cyclase is stuck on and cAMP rises. Protein kinase A then phosphorylates CFTR, causing chloride secretion into the lumen, and inhibits neutral NaCl absorption. Water follows osmotically, giving large volumes of isotonic, non-bloody 'rice-water' stool with no inflammation. Death comes from hypovolaemic shock, acidosis and potassium loss.

(c) The sodium-glucose co-transporter SGLT1 is independent of cAMP. Glucose absorption carries sodium, and water follows, so ORS can replace losses faster than they occur even while secretion continues. This is why ORS has saved so many lives in cholera.

(d) Because many organisms are killed by gastric acid, a large dose is usually needed, which is typically only achieved through heavily contaminated water or food rather than casual contact. Control should therefore focus on safe water (chlorination, a protected supply, closing the implicated collection point), sanitation and handwashing, together with oral cholera vaccine, early treatment centres and surveillance. Low gastric acidity raises individual risk.

questions.q:
A 28-year-old man presents to a London emergency department 9 days after returning from visiting family in Ghana. He did not take malaria prophylaxis. He has had fever and rigors for 3 days and is now drowsy and confused (GCS 12). Observations: temperature 39.8 C, pulse 118/min, blood pressure 102/60 mmHg. Bloods: haemoglobin 92 g/L, platelets 48 x 10^9/L, bilirubin raised, creatinine 210 micromol/L, glucose 3.1 mmol/L. A thin blood film shows ring forms of Plasmodium falciparum with 6% parasitaemia.

Explain the life cycle of P. falciparum in humans and how the parasite's biology accounts for this patient's clinical and laboratory features. Explain why non-immune travellers are at particular risk of severe disease.
markScheme: Transmission by a female Anopheles mosquito injecting sporozoites, which travel to hepatocytes (liver stage, about 1 week, no symptoms; falciparum forms no hypnozoites)
Merozoites invade red cells; repeated asexual cycles (about 48 h) with schizont rupture release pyrogenic material, causing fever and rigors via TNF and IL-1
Some parasites become gametocytes taken up by mosquitoes, completing transmission
P. falciparum invades red cells of all ages, so parasitaemia can be very high
PfEMP1 on knobs causes cytoadherence to endothelium and rosetting, so parasites sequester in the microvasculature, which explains cerebral malaria (impaired consciousness) and renal injury
Anaemia from haemolysis of infected and uninfected cells, splenic clearance and suppressed red-cell production; thrombocytopenia is typical
Hypoglycaemia from parasite glucose use, impaired gluconeogenesis and illness (also a known effect of quinine treatment)
Hyperbilirubinaemia from haemolysis and liver dysfunction; acute kidney injury from sequestration and haemoglobinuria
Non-immune travellers lack acquired (partial) immunity from repeated exposure, so disease can progress fast; people who have migrated lose immunity over time
Correctly identifies this as severe falciparum malaria needing urgent treatment, and that peripheral parasitaemia underestimates the sequestered biomass
questions.modelAnswer:
Infection begins when a female Anopheles mosquito takes a blood meal and injects sporozoites. These reach the liver within minutes and each invades a hepatocyte, where it multiplies into thousands of merozoites over about a week. This liver stage causes no symptoms. Unlike P. vivax and P. ovale, P. falciparum does not form dormant hypnozoites. Merozoites released into the blood invade red cells and pass through ring, trophozoite and schizont stages over roughly 48 hours. Schizonts then burst, releasing new merozoites and parasite products such as haemozoin and GPI anchors, which stimulate monocytes to release TNF and IL-1. This causes fever and rigors. A few parasites develop into gametocytes, which are taken up by mosquitoes to continue transmission.

Several features make P. falciparum especially dangerous. It invades red cells of any age, so parasitaemia can rise steeply. Mature infected cells carry PfEMP1 on surface knobs, which binds endothelial receptors such as ICAM-1 and CD36 and makes infected cells stick to uninfected cells (rosetting). Mature parasites therefore leave the circulation and collect in the microvasculature, avoiding the spleen. The film shows only ring forms, so the 6% peripheral parasitaemia underestimates the total parasite load.

Sequestration in brain capillaries, with local inflammation and disruption of the blood-brain barrier, explains his drowsiness (cerebral malaria). Sequestration in the kidney, together with haemoglobinuria and low perfusion, explains the acute kidney injury. Anaemia results from the destruction of infected red cells, accelerated clearance of uninfected cells and bone marrow suppression by cytokines. Thrombocytopenia is very common. Haemolysis and liver dysfunction raise bilirubin. Hypoglycaemia reflects parasite glucose consumption and impaired gluconeogenesis.

In endemic areas, repeated infections build partial immunity, including antibodies to variant surface antigens, that protects against severe disease. A visitor from the UK, or someone born in Ghana who has lived in the UK for years, has little or no such immunity, so disease can progress to organ failure within days. Impaired consciousness, renal impairment, hypoglycaemia and high parasitaemia make this severe falciparum malaria, which is a medical emergency needing intravenous artesunate (an artemisinin) and high-dependency care.

questions.q:
'Virulence is not a property of a microbe alone, but of the relationship between microbe and host.'

Discuss this statement, drawing on examples of bacterial, viral and fungal infection, opportunistic pathogens, commensals, and the role of host factors and microbial genetics.
markScheme: Defines pathogenicity and virulence (and measures such as ID50/LD50) and sets out the argument
Evidence for microbial determinants: toxins and virulence genes gained by horizontal transfer (CTX-phi in cholera, Shiga toxin phage in E. coli O157), capsules, molecular Koch's postulates
Evidence for host determinants: the same organism ranges from carriage to fatal disease (meningococcus, S. aureus, Candida), depending on immunity
Opportunists (Pneumocystis in HIV, Aspergillus in neutropenia, Pseudomonas in burns or CF) show that 'virulence' depends on host defences
Specific host defects reveal specific vulnerabilities: terminal complement deficiency with Neisseria, CGD with catalase-positive organisms, CCR5-delta32 resistance to R5 HIV
Damage can be caused by the host response itself (sepsis, superantigens, immunopathology in TB and hepatitis B); damage-response framework (Casadevall and Pirofski)
Context: site and route (commensal E. coli causing UTI), dose, microbiota and colonisation resistance (C. difficile after antibiotics), age and pregnancy
Counterpoint: some pathogens cause disease in almost any non-immune host (rabies, Ebola, smallpox), so microbial factors can dominate
Evolutionary view: virulence trade-offs with transmission, and host-pathogen co-evolution (e.g. myxoma in rabbits)
Reaches a reasoned conclusion: virulence is an emergent outcome of the interaction, with the balance of microbial and host contributions varying by organism
Well-structured argument, accurate examples and evaluation rather than description
questions.modelAnswer:
Pathogenicity is the capacity to cause disease, and virulence is its degree, often measured as the dose infecting or killing half of a test population (ID50 or LD50). The statement argues that virulence is a property of the interaction rather than of the organism. I will argue that this is largely right, while accepting that microbial factors sometimes dominate.

Microbial genetics clearly matter. Non-toxigenic V. cholerae causes little disease; acquiring the CTX-phi phage, which carries ctxAB, turns it into an epidemic pathogen. E. coli O157 became dangerous by gaining Shiga toxin genes from a phage. Unencapsulated pneumococci are largely avirulent. Falkow's molecular postulates formalise this: removing a virulence gene reduces disease.

Yet even these virulence factors only show their effect in a susceptible host. Neisseria meningitidis is carried harmlessly by many teenagers but causes fulminant sepsis in a person without bactericidal antibody, and the risk rises sharply with terminal complement deficiency or eculizumab therapy. Staphylococcus aureus and Candida albicans are commensals that become invasive after breaches of skin or mucosa, with indwelling devices, or in neutropenia. Opportunists show this most clearly: Pneumocystis jirovecii is harmless in people with normal immunity but lethal when CD4 counts fall in untreated HIV, and Aspergillus is dangerous mainly in neutropenia or chronic granulomatous disease. Host genetics can work the other way: people homozygous for CCR5-delta32 are highly resistant to R5-tropic HIV.

Much disease is also caused by the host's own response. Septic shock reflects a dysregulated cytokine response to LPS. TSST-1 causes harm by activating a large fraction of T cells, and liver damage in hepatitis B is largely caused by cytotoxic T cells. Casadevall and Pirofski's damage-response framework expresses this: disease is host damage, which can result from too weak a response (opportunists) or too strong a response (immunopathology). Context also matters: gut E. coli causes cystitis when it reaches the bladder, and C. difficile causes colitis when antibiotics remove colonisation resistance.

On the other side, rabies, Ebola and historically smallpox caused severe disease in almost any non-immune person, so the microbe's contribution can outweigh host variation. Evolution links the two: virulence often trades off against transmission, as when myxoma virus and Australian rabbits co-evolved towards intermediate virulence.

Virulence is therefore best seen as an outcome that emerges from the interaction between microbe, host and environment. How much the microbe or the host contributes differs between organisms, but neither alone determines it.

questions.q: Which immunoglobulin class crosses the placenta and gives the newborn passive protection?
options: IgA
IgM
IgE
IgG
questions.why: IgG is actively transported across the placenta by the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn). IgA is passed on in breast milk, while pentameric IgM is too large and has no transport receptor.

questions.q: A 22-year-old man has his second episode of invasive meningococcal disease in three years. His full blood count and immunoglobulins are normal. Deficiency of which component is most likely?
options: Terminal complement components (C5-C9)
C1 esterase inhibitor
Phagocyte NADPH oxidase
IgE
questions.why: The membrane attack complex is particularly important for killing Neisseria, so C5-C9 deficiency causes recurrent neisserial infection. C1 inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema, and NADPH oxidase deficiency (CGD) causes catalase-positive bacterial and fungal infections.

questions.q: A 4-year-old boy has had a Staphylococcus aureus liver abscess and Aspergillus pneumonia. His neutrophil count is normal and pus forms at infected sites. Which investigation is most likely to be abnormal?
options: Flow cytometry for CD18 on leucocytes
Dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow cytometry test of the neutrophil respiratory burst
CD40 ligand expression on activated T cells
Total haemolytic complement (CH50)
questions.why: Infections with catalase-positive organisms and Aspergillus, despite normal neutrophil numbers, point to chronic granulomatous disease (defective NADPH oxidase), which the DHR test detects. CD18 deficiency (leucocyte adhesion deficiency) causes infections without pus formation and delayed separation of the umbilical cord.

questions.q: Name three physical or chemical barriers that protect the body against infection, and explain briefly how each works.
markScheme: Skin: a tough keratinised layer that is dry and acidic, with fatty acids and antimicrobial peptides
Respiratory mucociliary escalator: mucus traps particles and cilia move them up and out of the airway
Chemical secretions, for example gastric acid killing swallowed organisms, or lysozyme in tears and saliva breaking down bacterial peptidoglycan (credit urine flow or commensal flora as alternatives)
questions.modelAnswer: Intact skin is a tough keratinised barrier. Its surface is dry, slightly acidic and carries fatty acids and antimicrobial peptides such as defensins, all of which discourage colonisation by pathogens. In the airways, mucus traps inhaled particles and microbes, and the beating cilia carry them up to the throat to be swallowed or coughed out. Smoking and cystic fibrosis impair this. The stomach's low pH kills most ingested organisms, and lysozyme in tears and saliva breaks down the peptidoglycan of bacterial cell walls.

questions.q: Explain why a protein-polysaccharide conjugate vaccine (e.g. Hib) protects infants better than a plain polysaccharide vaccine.
markScheme: Plain polysaccharides are T-independent antigens that cross-link B-cell receptors without T-cell help
Responses to T-independent antigens are poor under about 2 years of age, mostly IgM, short-lived and leave little memory
Conjugation to a protein carrier means B cells take up the conjugate and present carrier peptides on MHC class II to CD4 helper T cells
T-cell help (CD40L-CD40 and cytokines) drives germinal centres, class switching to IgG, affinity maturation and memory, and also reduces nasopharyngeal carriage, giving herd protection
questions.modelAnswer: Capsular polysaccharides have repeating units that cross-link B-cell receptors directly, so they act as T-independent antigens. Infants under about two years respond poorly to them, and the response is mainly low-affinity IgM with little memory. In a conjugate vaccine the polysaccharide is attached to a carrier protein such as tetanus toxoid. A B cell specific for the polysaccharide takes up the whole conjugate and presents carrier peptides on MHC class II to helper T cells. Their help, through CD40L and cytokines, starts a germinal centre reaction with class switching to IgG, affinity maturation and memory B cells. Mucosal immunity also reduces carriage, which protects unvaccinated people too.

questions.q: A carpenter gets a splinter in his finger that carries Staphylococcus aureus into the dermis. Describe the innate immune events in the first few hours that limit the infection.
markScheme: Resident macrophages and mast cells recognise PAMPs (e.g. lipoteichoic acid and lipoproteins via TLR2) and release TNF, IL-1, chemokines such as CXCL8, and histamine
Complement is activated (alternative and lectin pathways): C3b opsonises, and C5a attracts neutrophils and raises vascular permeability
Vasodilation and increased permeability cause redness, heat and swelling; plasma proteins and fluid enter the tissue
Neutrophils roll (selectins), adhere firmly (integrins binding ICAM-1) and migrate out of vessels along chemokine gradients

Neutrophils phagocytose opsonised bacteria and kill them by the respiratory burst (NADPH oxidase), granule enzymes and NETs; pus forms. Dendritic cells carry antigen to lymph nodes to start adaptive immunity
questions.modelAnswer: Tissue macrophages and mast cells detect staphylococcal PAMPs such as lipoteichoic acid and lipoproteins through TLR2. They release TNF, IL-1, chemokines including CXCL8, and histamine. Complement is activated on the bacterial surface by the alternative and lectin pathways: C3b coats the bacteria and C5a attracts neutrophils. Local vessels dilate and become leaky, which produces redness, heat and swelling. Endothelium expresses selectins and ICAM-1, so neutrophils roll, stick firmly through their integrins and squeeze into the tissue. There they ingest opsonised bacteria through Fc and complement receptors and kill them with reactive oxygen species and granule enzymes. Dead neutrophils form pus. Dendritic cells carry antigen to the draining lymph node.

questions.q:
A previously healthy 20-year-old student develops influenza confirmed by PCR. Day 0: infection. Day 2: abrupt fever, myalgia and dry cough. Day 4: symptoms peak. Day 8: she is recovering and nasal viral shedding has largely stopped. Paired serology shows influenza-specific IgM detectable at around day 7, and IgG rising more than four-fold between day 3 and day 21. Two years later she is exposed to the same strain and remains well.

Describe the innate and adaptive immune responses that explain this timeline. Explain the roles of interferons, NK cells, CD8 and CD4 T cells, and antibodies, and why she was protected on re-exposure.
markScheme: Infected airway epithelium detects viral RNA (RIG-I, TLR3/7) and produces type I interferons, which induce an antiviral state in nearby cells
Cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF, interferons) explain the early fever and myalgia, not direct viral damage alone
NK cells kill infected cells with reduced MHC class I early on, before T cells appear, and produce IFN-gamma
Dendritic cells carry antigen to lymph nodes and prime naive T cells (peptide-MHC, co-stimulation, cytokines); clonal expansion takes several days
CD8 cytotoxic T cells recognise viral peptides on MHC class I and kill infected cells (perforin, granzymes) from about day 5-7, explaining clearance
CD4 Th1 and Tfh cells support CD8 responses and B cells; germinal centres generate class switching and affinity maturation
IgM appears first, followed by high-affinity IgG; neutralising anti-haemagglutinin antibody (and mucosal IgA) blocks reinfection
Memory B cells, long-lived plasma cells and memory T cells give rapid, strong secondary responses, so re-exposure to the same strain is controlled before symptoms
Notes the caveat that drift would erode this protection
Logical chronological structure linked to the timeline
questions.modelAnswer:
Within hours of infection, airway epithelial cells detect viral RNA through cytosolic RIG-I and endosomal TLR3 and TLR7. They secrete type I interferons (IFN-alpha and IFN-beta), which put neighbouring cells into an antiviral state, for example by inducing proteins that block viral replication, and which increase MHC class I expression. Interferons, IL-1, IL-6 and TNF act on the hypothalamus and muscle, so the sudden fever and myalgia on day 2 largely reflect the innate response.

NK cells arrive in the first few days. They kill infected cells that have reduced MHC class I and secrete IFN-gamma, which slows viral spread while adaptive immunity develops.

Meanwhile dendritic cells pick up viral antigen and travel to the mediastinal lymph nodes. Naive CD8 and CD4 T cells that recognise viral peptides on MHC class I or II, and receive co-stimulation through CD28 and polarising cytokines, multiply over several days. This lag explains why symptoms peak around day 4. Cytotoxic CD8 T cells then travel to the lung from about day 5-7, recognise viral peptides on infected cells and kill them with perforin and granzymes. Together with antibody, this clears the virus, so shedding has largely stopped by day 8.

CD4 Th1 cells provide IFN-gamma and help CD8 responses, and T-follicular-helper cells drive B cells in germinal centres. The first antibody is IgM, detectable around day 7. Class switching and affinity maturation then produce high-affinity IgG and mucosal IgA, so IgG titres rise over the following weeks, which explains the four-fold rise between days 3 and 21. Antibodies against haemagglutinin neutralise the virus by blocking its attachment to sialic acid.

After recovery she keeps long-lived plasma cells that maintain neutralising antibody, together with memory B and T cells. On re-exposure to the same strain, existing antibody neutralises most virus at the mucosa and memory cells respond within days, faster and more strongly than before, so infection is controlled before symptoms appear.
