Antigenic drift would reduce this protection against a later, changed strain, which is why influenza vaccines are updated.

questions.q:
A 34-year-old man presents with three weeks of increasing breathlessness on exertion, dry cough and weight loss. He has oral candidiasis. His oxygen saturation falls from 95% at rest to 86% on walking. Chest X-ray shows bilateral perihilar interstitial shadowing. An HIV test is positive, his CD4 count is 120 cells/microlitre (normal roughly 500-1500) and his viral load is high. Bronchoalveolar lavage confirms Pneumocystis jirovecii.

Explain how HIV infection leads to this degree of immunodeficiency. Relate the loss of specific immune functions to the infections seen and to others that may occur at lower CD4 counts. Explain which defences remain relatively preserved, and what happens to immune function once effective antiretroviral therapy begins.
markScheme: HIV gp120 binds CD4 plus CCR5 or CXCR4, infecting CD4 T cells, macrophages and dendritic cells; reverse transcription and integration establish latent reservoirs
Mechanisms of CD4 depletion: direct cytopathic effect, pyroptosis of abortively infected cells, CD8 killing of infected cells, chronic immune activation and exhaustion
Early, massive depletion of CD4 T cells in gut-associated lymphoid tissue, with microbial translocation driving chronic activation
Loss of CD4 help impairs macrophage activation (Th1/IFN-gamma), CD8 T-cell maintenance, B-cell class switching and Th17-mediated mucosal antifungal defence

Links infections to CD4 thresholds: oral candida and TB occur earlier; Pneumocystis typically below 200; toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal meningitis below about 100; CMV retinitis and disseminated MAC below about 50
Relatively preserved: neutrophils, complement and barrier defences initially, so pyogenic bacterial infections are less dominant (although pneumococcal disease is increased)
B-cell dysregulation: hypergammaglobulinaemia but poor specific responses to new antigens and vaccines
Antiretroviral therapy suppresses replication and CD4 counts recover; immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) may unmask or worsen opportunistic infections
Notes that the latent reservoir persists, so therapy is lifelong
Integrates immunology with the clinical features and evaluates rather than lists
questions.modelAnswer:
HIV uses gp120 to bind CD4 and then a co-receptor, usually CCR5 early in infection and sometimes CXCR4 later, and gp41 drives fusion. Its targets are CD4 T cells, macrophages and dendritic cells. Reverse transcriptase makes a DNA copy that integrase inserts into the host genome, creating a latent reservoir in resting memory T cells.

CD4 T cells are lost by several routes. Productively infected cells die from viral cytopathic effects and are killed by cytotoxic T cells. Many bystander cells that are only abortively infected die by pyroptosis. Persistent viral replication, together with microbial products leaking across a damaged gut mucosa, keeps the immune system chronically activated, which exhausts T cells and wears down lymphoid tissue. Within weeks of infection, gut-associated lymphoid tissue loses most of its CD4 T cells, especially Th17 cells. Over years, production cannot keep up and blood CD4 counts fall.

CD4 T cells coordinate much of adaptive immunity, so their loss has broad effects. Without Th1-derived IFN-gamma, macrophages cannot kill intracellular organisms efficiently. Without Th17 cells, mucosal antifungal defence fails, causing oral candidiasis. Without T-cell help, CD8 memory and B-cell class switching are impaired. Infections appear in a rough order as CD4 counts fall. Tuberculosis and oral candida occur at relatively high counts. Pneumocystis pneumonia typically appears below 200 cells/microlitre, as here. Cerebral toxoplasmosis and cryptococcal meningitis tend to occur below about 100, and CMV retinitis and disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex below about 50. His count of 120 means he is at risk of the next group, and prophylaxis against further opportunistic infections would be considered.

Neutrophils, complement and epithelial barriers are relatively spared at first, so overwhelming pyogenic infection is not the main early feature, although invasive pneumococcal disease is more common. B cells are polyclonally activated, which produces hypergammaglobulinaemia, but specific antibody responses to new antigens and vaccines are poor.

Combination antiretroviral therapy suppresses viral replication, after which CD4 counts and pathogen-specific responses gradually recover. A recovering immune system can react strongly to antigens already present, causing immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome. This is why the timing of antiretroviral therapy is carefully planned in some opportunistic infections, such as cryptococcal and tuberculous meningitis. The integrated reservoir is not eliminated, so treatment is lifelong. With a sustained undetectable viral load, life expectancy approaches normal and sexual transmission does not occur.

questions.q:
A 68-year-old woman is admitted with a two-day history of dysuria and loin pain and is now confused. Temperature 39.1 C, heart rate 124/min, respiratory rate 28/min, blood pressure 84/48 mmHg, lactate 4.6 mmol/L, platelets 90 x 10^9/L and creatinine raised. Blood cultures grow Escherichia coli. After fluid resuscitation she still needs noradrenaline to maintain blood pressure. She survives the ICU stay, but in week two she develops a ventilator-associated Candida bloodstream infection and reactivation of herpes simplex virus.

(a) Calculate her mean arterial pressure and state whether she meets the Sepsis-3 criteria for septic shock. (b) Explain the immunological mechanisms that lead from Gram-negative bacteraemia to organ dysfunction and shock. (c) Explain why she later became vulnerable to secondary infections. (d) Evaluate why drugs that block single inflammatory mediators have largely failed in clinical trials of sepsis.
markScheme: MAP is about (2 x 48 + 84)/3 = 60 mmHg; persistent hypotension needing vasopressors to keep MAP at or above 65, plus lactate above 2 despite fluids, meets septic shock criteria; SOFA rise of 2 or more is implied
LPS (lipid A) binds LBP and CD14 and signals through TLR4/MD-2 via MyD88 and TRIF, activating NF-kappaB and IRF3; DAMPs from damaged tissue amplify the response
TNF, IL-1 and IL-6 cause fever, endothelial activation and the acute phase response; complement C5a and neutrophil activation add to tissue injury
Nitric oxide-mediated vasodilation, glycocalyx damage and capillary leak cause distributive shock; myocardial depression may contribute

Tissue factor expression and impaired anticoagulant pathways cause DIC and microthrombosis (thrombocytopenia); poor microcirculation and mitochondrial dysfunction raise lactate and cause organ failure (confusion, AKI)
Sepsis-induced immunosuppression: lymphocyte apoptosis, monocyte deactivation (reduced HLA-DR), increased IL-10, T-cell exhaustion (PD-1) and regulatory T cells
Clinical consequences: secondary nosocomial infections (Candida, resistant bacteria) and viral reactivation (HSV, CMV), aggravated by lines, ventilation and broad-spectrum antibiotics

Failure of single-target trials: redundant and overlapping cytokine networks; heterogeneous patients and timing; hyper- and hypo-inflammatory phases coexist; e.g. anti-TNF antibodies and the TLR4 antagonist eritoran did not improve survival
Future directions: stratifying patients (endotypes, biomarkers), immunostimulation for immunosuppressed patients, precision trials
Coherent structure, correct calculation and critical evaluation
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) MAP is approximately (2 x diastolic + systolic) / 3 = (96 + 84) / 3 = 60 mmHg. Sepsis-3 defines septic shock as sepsis with hypotension needing vasopressors to keep MAP at 65 mmHg or above, and lactate above 2 mmol/L, despite adequate fluid resuscitation. Her need for noradrenaline after fluids and her lactate of 4.6 meet this definition. Her confusion, low platelets and raised creatinine show organ dysfunction consistent with a SOFA rise of at least 2.

(b) Lipid A of E. coli LPS is carried by LPS-binding protein to CD14 and signals through TLR4/MD-2. The MyD88 pathway activates NF-kappaB and the TRIF pathway activates IRF3, leading to large amounts of TNF, IL-1, IL-6 and type I interferon. Damaged cells release DAMPs, such as HMGB1, that feed the response further. Complement activation produces C5a, which primes neutrophils, and activated neutrophils damage endothelium. Endothelial activation, with inducible nitric oxide synthase, vasodilation, shedding of the glycocalyx and capillary leak, causes distributive shock, and cytokine-mediated myocardial depression adds to it. Monocytes and endothelium express tissue factor while natural anticoagulants such as protein C are consumed, causing microvascular thrombosis and thrombocytopenia (DIC). Poor microcirculatory flow and mitochondrial dysfunction raise lactate and cause kidney injury and encephalopathy.

(c) Inflammation in sepsis is accompanied by profound immunosuppression. Widespread apoptosis of lymphocytes and dendritic cells, monocytes with reduced HLA-DR expression that respond poorly to new stimuli, high IL-10, T-cell exhaustion with PD-1 upregulation and more regulatory T cells all impair host defence. Together with central lines, mechanical ventilation and broad-spectrum antibiotics disrupting her microbiota, this explains invasive candidiasis and reactivation of latent herpesviruses in week two. Much late sepsis mortality is linked to this phase.

(d) Trials of anti-TNF antibodies, IL-1 receptor antagonist and the TLR4 antagonist eritoran did not reduce mortality. Cytokine networks are redundant, so blocking one mediator is compensated by others. By the time patients reach hospital the initial cytokine surge may already be over. Patients with 'sepsis' differ widely in pathogen, source, age, comorbidity and immune state; some are hyperinflammatory and others immunoparalysed, and the same drug may help one group and harm another. The broad clinical definition used to enrol patients therefore mixes different biological states. Current research aims to identify sepsis subgroups (endotypes) using biomarkers, matching anti-inflammatory or immunostimulatory treatment to each patient's immune state. Until then, management rests on early source control, appropriate antimicrobials and organ support.

questions.q:
'The most effective vaccines are those that most closely mimic natural infection.'

Discuss this statement with reference to live attenuated, inactivated, toxoid, subunit, conjugate and mRNA vaccines. Consider the immune mechanisms each engages, their strengths and limitations, and the groups in whom each is appropriate.
markScheme: Natural infection engages innate sensing (PAMPs, danger signals), antigen in its native form and location, CD4 and CD8 T cells, antibody and long-lived memory
Live attenuated vaccines (MMR, varicella, BCG, oral rotavirus) replicate, give strong cellular and humoral immunity and often lifelong protection after one or two doses
Limits of live vaccines: risk in severe immunosuppression and pregnancy; rare reversion (e.g. vaccine-derived poliovirus from oral polio vaccine); cold chain

Inactivated and subunit vaccines (inactivated polio, hepatitis B, HPV) are safe in the immunocompromised but mainly induce antibody; they need adjuvants and boosters; HPV gives very high efficacy without mimicking infection
Toxoids (tetanus, diphtheria) give protection that natural infection does not, because tetanus infection does not reliably induce immunity
Conjugate vaccines outperform natural polysaccharide exposure in infants by recruiting T-cell help, and reduce carriage, giving herd effects

mRNA vaccines produce antigen inside the host's own cells (MHC class I and II presentation), induce strong antibody and T-cell responses and can be updated quickly; waning protection against infection with variant evolution
Mucosal immunity: injected vaccines may give less secretory IgA than natural or mucosal infection (oral vs injected polio)
Evaluation: 'effective' depends on the goal (preventing disease vs transmission, individual vs population) and on safety; better vaccines can be engineered beyond mimicking infection
Balanced conclusion and clear structure
questions.modelAnswer:
Natural infection is powerful because it delivers antigen in its native form, at the right site, with innate danger signals. It activates dendritic cells, primes CD4 and CD8 T cells and generates neutralising antibody, mucosal IgA and long-lived memory. The statement has some truth, but the best vaccines often do better than infection in specific ways.

Live attenuated vaccines come closest to infection. Measles, mumps and rubella vaccine strains replicate, present antigen through MHC class I and II, and give durable humoral and cellular immunity after two doses. Oral polio vaccine also induced intestinal IgA that blocked transmission. However, replication is also their weakness: they are generally contraindicated in severe immunosuppression and pregnancy, and oral polio vaccine can rarely revert to neurovirulence, causing vaccine-derived polio. This is one reason the UK uses inactivated polio vaccine.

Inactivated and subunit vaccines mimic infection far less, yet some are highly effective. Recombinant HPV virus-like particles produce antibody levels well above those after natural infection, which itself often fails to protect, and have greatly reduced cervical precancer. Hepatitis B surface antigen vaccine prevents chronic infection. These vaccines are safe in immunocompromised patients but mainly induce antibody and often need adjuvants and boosters.

Toxoids directly contradict the statement. Tetanus toxin is so potent that disease occurs at doses too small to immunise, so survivors still need vaccination. A toxoid separates immunogenicity from toxicity.

Conjugate vaccines also outperform nature in infants. Naturally encountered capsular polysaccharides are T-independent and give poor responses before about two years of age, whereas conjugation recruits T-cell help, producing class-switched memory and reduced carriage. Hib conjugate vaccine dramatically reduced Hib meningitis, partly through herd protection.

mRNA vaccines mimic one key feature of viral infection: antigen is made inside host cells, so it is presented on both MHC classes and drives strong antibody and T-cell responses. They can also be updated quickly. Their protection against infection wanes faster than protection against severe disease as variants evolve, and injected vaccines induce limited mucosal IgA.

The statement therefore oversimplifies. Mimicking infection helps with breadth, cellular immunity and durability, but effectiveness depends on the goal (preventing disease or preventing transmission), on safety in the target group, and on whether natural infection itself protects. Rational design can now improve on nature rather than simply copy it.

questions.q: An infection has a basic reproduction number (R0) of 5. In a simple homogeneous model, what proportion of the population must be immune for sustained transmission to stop?
A rapid test has sensitivity 90% and specificity 95%. It is used to screen 1,000 people in a population where the prevalence is 2%. What is the positive predictive value, to the nearest whole number?
questions.why: 20 people have the disease, of whom 18 test positive (TP). Of the 980 without disease, 5% (49) test positive (FP). PPV = 18/(18+49) = 18/67, about 27%. At low prevalence, false positives outnumber true positives.

questions.q: A vaccine is 90% effective at preventing transmission of an infection whose R0 is 6. Assuming homogeneous mixing, what is the minimum vaccination coverage needed to prevent sustained spread?
options: About 93%
About 83%
About 75%
It cannot be achieved even at 100% coverage
questions.why: HIT = 1 - 1/6 = 0.833. Critical coverage = HIT / effectiveness = 0.833 / 0.9, about 0.93 (93%). Elimination would be impossible only if effectiveness were below the herd immunity threshold.

questions.q: Define incidence and prevalence. Explain why the number of people living with HIV in the UK has continued to rise even though new diagnoses have fallen.
markScheme: Incidence: new cases arising in a population at risk over a defined period (a rate or risk)
Prevalence: the proportion of a population with the condition at a point in time (or over a period)
In a steady state, prevalence is roughly incidence x average duration of disease
Effective antiretroviral therapy has greatly extended survival, so duration has increased; even with lower incidence, more people are living with HIV (and the population is ageing)
questions.modelAnswer: Incidence is the number of new cases arising in a population at risk over a stated period, for example new HIV diagnoses per 100,000 per year. Prevalence is the proportion of the population living with the condition at a particular time. When conditions are fairly stable, prevalence is approximately incidence multiplied by average disease duration. Effective antiretroviral therapy has turned HIV into a long-term condition with near-normal life expectancy, so duration has increased greatly. Fewer new infections are being added, but far fewer people are leaving the prevalent pool through death, so the total number living with HIV keeps rising.

questions.q: In a household study of a respiratory infection, 40 households each contained one index case. These households had 130 other members, of whom 10 had documented immunity from previous vaccination. Over the following two incubation periods, 36 further household members became ill. Calculate the secondary attack rate and explain two methodological points that affect its interpretation.
markScheme: Susceptible contacts = 130 - 10 = 120
Immune contacts are excluded from the denominator because they are not at risk; including them would underestimate transmissibility (36/130 = 27.7%)

Co-primary cases (infected from the same outside source at the same time) and tertiary cases should be excluded, which is why a defined time window based on the incubation period is used; contacts infected outside the household would inflate the estimate
questions.modelAnswer: The denominator should include only susceptible contacts: 130 - 10 = 120. SAR = 36/120 = 30%. Immune household members cannot become secondary cases, so including them (36/130 = 27.7%) would understate how readily the infection spreads. The time window matters too. Cases appearing very soon after the index case may be co-primary cases from the same outside exposure, while later cases may be tertiary cases or infections acquired outside the home. Limiting counting to a window based on the incubation period, and checking for exposures outside the household, makes the SAR a better estimate of household transmission.

questions.q: For an infection with R0 = 2.5 in a fully susceptible, well-mixed population with no interventions, calculate the herd immunity threshold. Explain why the final proportion infected in an unmitigated epidemic is expected to be much larger than this threshold, and give one reason why real epidemics may differ from this prediction.
markScheme: At the HIT, Re = 1 and the number currently infected peaks; new infections do not stop there
Many people are still infectious at the peak, so transmission continues (at Re below 1) and more susceptible people are infected: overshoot
In the simple SIR model, final size z satisfies z = 1 - e^(-R0 z), giving about 89% for R0 = 2.5
Real differences: heterogeneous mixing and susceptibility (immunity concentrated in high-contact people lowers the effective threshold), behaviour change, interventions, waning immunity, seasonality
questions.modelAnswer: HIT = 1 - 1/2.5 = 0.6, so 60%. Reaching this threshold only means Re has fallen to 1, which is when the number of people currently infected peaks, not the end of the epidemic. At that point many people are still infectious, and each still infects close to one other person as Re slowly falls further, so infections continue well past 60%. This is called overshoot. In the basic SIR model the final size z is given by z = 1 - e^(-R0 z), which for R0 = 2.5 gives about 89%. Real epidemics often differ. Mixing is uneven: high-contact people are infected first, so immunity builds up where it matters most. People also change their behaviour, interventions are introduced and immunity may wane.

questions.q:
After a wedding reception attended by 150 guests, many develop abdominal cramps and watery diarrhoea. The local health protection team interview 120 guests. Fifty-two report illness meeting the case definition. Symptoms began a median of 14 hours after the meal (range 8-22 hours), and most resolved within 24 hours. Vomiting and fever were uncommon. Food histories:

- Chicken curry: 80 ate it, 48 became ill; 40 did not, 4 became ill.
- Rice salad: 60 ate it, 30 became ill; 60 did not, 22 became ill.

The curry was cooked the day before in a large pot, cooled slowly at room temperature and reheated.

(a) Calculate the overall attack rate and the food-specific attack rates and relative risks. (b) Interpret the epidemic curve information and suggest a likely organism. (c) Discuss limitations of this investigation and outline control measures.
markScheme: Overall attack rate = 52/120 = 43.3%
Chicken curry: 48/80 = 60% vs 4/40 = 10%; RR = 6.0
Rice salad: 30/60 = 50% vs 22/60 = 36.7%; RR about 1.36
Curry is the most likely vehicle: high RR, and only 4 cases did not eat it; the weak rice association is probably confounding (people eating curry also ate rice); stratified analysis would test this
All onsets within one incubation period with a single peak suggest a point-source outbreak

Incubation 8-22 h, cramps and diarrhoea without much vomiting or fever, and slow cooling and reheating of a meat stew suggest Clostridium perfringens (spores germinate during slow cooling; enterotoxin released in the gut)
Limitations: 30 guests not interviewed (selection bias), recall bias, misclassification of cases, small numbers, need for confidence intervals; RR calculation suits a defined cohort
Microbiological confirmation: stool samples, food remnants, food handler interviews; environmental health inspection
Control: safe cooling and reheating, temperature control, staff training, enforcement action, and communicating findings and lessons learned
Clear presentation of calculations and reasoning
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Overall attack rate = 52/120 = 43.3%.
Chicken curry: attack rate among those who ate it = 48/80 = 60%; among those who did not = 4/40 = 10%; RR = 60/10 = 6.0.
Rice salad: 30/60 = 50% vs 22/60 = 36.7%; RR = 50/36.7, about 1.36.

Curry is strongly associated with illness: eating it increases the risk six-fold, and only 4 of 52 cases (8%) had not eaten it. The weak link with rice salad is probably confounding, because most guests who ate rice also ate curry. Stratifying the rice analysis by curry consumption, or using logistic regression, would test this. Chi-squared tests or confidence intervals would show whether the associations could be due to chance.

(b) All cases began within one incubation-period range (8-22 hours) around a single peak, which fits a point-source outbreak from one meal rather than person-to-person spread, which would produce later waves. The clinical picture of cramps and watery diarrhoea with little vomiting or fever, a median incubation of about 14 hours and rapid recovery, together with a large meat dish cooled slowly and reheated, strongly suggests Clostridium perfringens. Its spores survive cooking, germinate and multiply as food cools slowly through warm temperatures, and the vegetative cells release enterotoxin in the gut as they sporulate. The diarrhoeal form of Bacillus cereus (often linked to rice dishes) is the main differential and would be distinguished by laboratory testing, while staphylococcal toxin causes earlier onset (a few hours) with prominent vomiting.

(c) Limitations: 30 guests (20%) were not interviewed, and if response was related to illness, attack rates are biased. Food histories are subject to recall bias, especially once guests have heard which dish is suspected. Case definitions based on symptoms may misclassify people. Numbers are small, so estimates are imprecise. A cohort design is appropriate because the guest list defines the population at risk. Confirmation requires stool testing (for C. perfringens enterotoxin or typing), testing of any remaining food, and interviews with the caterer about how the food was handled.

Control: the local authority environmental health officers should inspect the caterer, stop unsafe practice and enforce rapid cooling, refrigeration and thorough reheating, with staff training and HACCP-based procedures. Findings should be communicated to guests, the caterer and public health partners, and the outbreak formally closed with a report.

questions.q:
A secondary school has 800 pupils. One pupil develops measles after a holiday abroad. Measles has an R0 of about 15 in this setting. Records show 85% of pupils have had two doses of MMR. Assume two doses prevent infection in 97% of recipients, and that all other pupils are susceptible (ignore past infection).

(a) Calculate the herd immunity threshold, the proportion of pupils immune, the effective reproduction number, the approximate number of susceptible pupils, and the vaccination coverage needed to prevent sustained transmission. (b) Interpret these results. (c) Outline the public health response, including measures for vulnerable contacts. (d) Explain why averages for the school may underestimate outbreak risk.
markScheme: Proportion immune = 0.85 x 0.97 = 0.8245 (82.5%); susceptible = 17.55%
Re = 15 x 0.1755, about 2.6, so the outbreak can grow
Susceptible pupils = 800 x 0.1755, about 140
Critical coverage = 0.933 / 0.97, about 0.962 (96%), which exceeds current coverage
Response: notify (measles is notifiable, on clinical suspicion), confirm by oral fluid or PCR testing, identify contacts, exclude cases for 4 days after rash onset
Offer MMR to unvaccinated or partially vaccinated pupils and staff (post-exposure MMR within about 3 days may prevent or modify illness); catch-up campaign
Vulnerable contacts (immunosuppressed, susceptible pregnant women, young infants) assessed for human normal immunoglobulin (passive immunity) rather than live vaccine
Clustering: unvaccinated pupils often cluster in friendship or community groups, so local Re is higher than the average; heterogeneity and overdispersion
Communicate with parents sensitively; address hesitancy
Logical working and interpretation
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Herd immunity threshold = 1 - 1/15 = 0.933, i.e. 93.3%.
Proportion immune = coverage x effectiveness = 0.85 x 0.97 = 0.8245 (82.5%), so 17.55% are susceptible.
Re = R0 x susceptible proportion = 15 x 0.1755, about 2.6.
Susceptible pupils = 800 x 0.1755, about 140.
Critical coverage = HIT / effectiveness = 0.933 / 0.97, about 0.962, so about 96% of pupils need two doses.

(b) Population immunity (82.5%) is well below the 93% threshold, so each case would on average infect about 2.6 others at the start. A school outbreak is likely, with up to about 140 susceptible pupils plus susceptible staff and family members. Because measles is so transmissible, even 85% two-dose coverage is not enough; the WHO target of 95% coverage with two doses reflects this.

(c) Measles is notifiable, so the clinician must notify the local authority's proper officer (via UKHSA) on clinical suspicion without waiting for results. The diagnosis is confirmed by oral fluid or PCR testing. The health protection team identifies contacts and checks vaccination status. Cases are excluded from school until 4 days after rash onset. Unvaccinated and partially vaccinated pupils and staff are offered MMR. Given within about 72 hours of exposure it may prevent illness, and in any case it protects against later exposures, so a catch-up campaign is worthwhile. Contacts who cannot have a live vaccine and are at high risk of severe measles, such as immunosuppressed children, susceptible pregnant women and young infants, are assessed for human normal immunoglobulin, which gives immediate passive protection. Clear, non-judgemental communication with families, using trusted local voices, helps encourage uptake. Surveillance continues for two incubation periods after the last case.

(d) These figures assume homogeneous mixing. In practice, unvaccinated pupils often cluster within particular year groups, friendship networks, faith communities or families who decline vaccination. Within such clusters the susceptible proportion may be 50% or more, giving a local Re far above 2.6 and explosive spread, even if school-wide coverage looks reasonable. Transmission is also overdispersed, with some cases infecting many others. Two-dose effectiveness and records may be imperfect, and some protection may wane. Coverage should therefore be examined by subgroup, and outbreak control should target clusters of susceptible pupils.

questions.q:
A new lateral flow antigen test for a respiratory virus has sensitivity 80% and specificity 99.5% compared with PCR. Two uses are proposed:

(A) Mass testing of 100,000 asymptomatic people in a town where PCR prevalence is 0.5%.
(B) Testing 1,000 people with symptoms attending a clinic, where prevalence is 20%.

(a) For each setting, construct a 2x2 table and calculate the positive and negative predictive values. (b) Calculate the positive and negative likelihood ratios. (c) Discuss what these results mean for policy, including confirmatory testing, communicating results, and whether PCR is the right reference standard for controlling infection.
markScheme: Setting A: 500 infected; TP = 400, FN = 100; 99,500 uninfected; FP about 498, TN about 99,002
Setting A: PPV = 400/898, about 45%; NPV = 99,002/99,102, about 99.9%
Setting B: 200 infected; TP = 160, FN = 40; 800 uninfected; FP = 4, TN = 796; PPV = 160/164, about 97.6%; NPV = 796/836, about 95.2%
LR+ = 0.8/0.005 = 160; LR- = 0.2/0.995, about 0.20; likelihood ratios do not depend on prevalence, but predictive values do
In low-prevalence mass testing, more than half of positives are false, so confirmatory PCR is needed; a negative result does not exclude infection (100 missed)
In the symptomatic clinic a positive is highly reliable; a negative still misses 1 in 5 infections, so false reassurance needs safety-netting or a repeat test
Reference standard issue: PCR detects RNA after infectiousness has ended, so lateral flow sensitivity for infectious people may be higher than 80%; spectrum bias
Serial testing, speed and convenience may outweigh lower sensitivity for public health purposes (frequency and turnaround over accuracy)
Harms and costs: unnecessary isolation and anxiety from false positives; false reassurance from negatives
Balanced, setting-specific recommendation
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Setting A (100,000 people, prevalence 0.5%): 500 infected and 99,500 uninfected.
TP = 0.8 x 500 = 400; FN = 100.
FP = 0.005 x 99,500, about 498; TN, about 99,002.
PPV = 400 / (400 + 498), about 44.5%. NPV = 99,002 / (99,002 + 100), about 99.9%.

Setting B (1,000 people, prevalence 20%): 200 infected and 800 uninfected.
TP = 160; FN = 40. FP = 0.005 x 800 = 4; TN = 796.
PPV = 160/164, about 97.6%. NPV = 796/836, about 95.2%.

(b) LR+ = sensitivity / (1 - specificity) = 0.8 / 0.005 = 160. LR- = (1 - sensitivity) / specificity = 0.2 / 0.995, about 0.20. Likelihood ratios are properties of the test and stay the same in both settings. The predictive values differ because the pre-test probabilities differ.

(c) In mass asymptomatic testing, even with 99.5% specificity, more than half of positive results are false, because the uninfected population is so large. Without confirmation, about 500 people would isolate unnecessarily and contact tracing would be wasted. Confirmatory PCR, or a repeat lateral flow test, is therefore sensible. The NPV looks reassuring, but 100 infected people would be told they are negative. Results should be explained as 'probably not infectious now', not as clearance.

In symptomatic people, a positive result is very likely to be true and can be acted on without confirmation. A negative result, however, still misses one in five infections, and NPV is only about 95%, so people with symptoms should still take precautions or retest.

The reference standard also matters. PCR can detect viral RNA for days or weeks after someone stops being infectious, so a lateral flow test that is 'false negative' against PCR may in fact be correct about infectiousness. Its sensitivity for detecting infectious people may be higher than 80%. Accuracy studies in symptomatic patients may also overestimate performance in asymptomatic people with lower viral loads (spectrum bias). For public health purposes, cheap, fast, frequent testing can reduce transmission more than a more sensitive test that is slow and done rarely.

Overall, the test is well suited to symptomatic clinics, with negative results interpreted cautiously. Mass asymptomatic screening at 0.5% prevalence can be justified only with confirmation of positives, serial testing, clear communication and attention to the costs of false positives.

questions.q:
In the first weeks of an outbreak of a novel respiratory virus, confirmed case numbers double every 4 days. Contact-tracing data suggest a mean serial interval of 5 days, and about 40% of transmission occurs before the infector develops symptoms. Analysis of clusters shows that around 15% of cases cause about 80% of onward transmission.

(a) Estimate the exponential growth rate r and use two simple approximations to estimate the reproduction number R (state the assumption behind each). (b) Use your estimates to calculate a range for the herd immunity threshold. (c) Explain what pre-symptomatic transmission and overdispersion imply for control strategies such as isolating symptomatic cases, contact tracing (forward and backward) and restrictions on gatherings. (d) Critically evaluate the reliability of these early estimates.
markScheme: r = ln 2 / doubling time = 0.693 / 4, about 0.17 per day
If the generation interval is fixed (all transmission at exactly 5 days): R = e^(rT) = e^(0.87), about 2.4
If the generation interval is exponentially distributed with mean 5 days: R = 1 + rT, about 1.9; the true value depends on the distribution's shape and probably lies between these

Pre-symptomatic transmission (latent period shorter than incubation period) means isolating symptomatic cases alone cannot stop spread; tracing and quarantining contacts must be fast, and testing of contacts is needed

Overdispersion (low k): most cases infect few or none, so many introductions die out by chance; transmission concentrates in superspreading events and high-risk settings, so restricting large indoor gatherings and ventilation are efficient
Backward tracing (finding who infected the case and where) is efficient under overdispersion because it finds clusters; forward tracing interrupts onward chains
Serial interval is not the same as the generation interval (it can be shorter, or even negative, with pre-symptomatic spread); using it introduces bias
Biases in early data: growth in confirmed cases reflects growth in testing; reporting delays; small, biased cluster samples; right-censoring of serial intervals
Estimates should be given as ranges with uncertainty, updated as data improve, and triangulated with hospital admissions, deaths and seroprevalence
Sophisticated structure with explicit assumptions
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) r = ln 2 / doubling time = 0.693 / 4, about 0.173 per day. The relationship between r and R depends on the generation interval distribution, approximated here by the 5-day serial interval (rT, about 0.87).
- If every case transmits exactly 5 days after being infected (a fixed interval), R = e^(rT) = e^0.87, about 2.4.
- If generation intervals are exponentially distributed with a mean of 5 days, as in a simple SIR model, R = 1 + rT, about 1.9.
Real generation intervals lie between these two extremes, so R is probably about 1.9-2.4.

(b) HIT = 1 - 1/R gives 1 - 1/1.9, about 47%, to 1 - 1/2.4, about 58%. This assumes homogeneous mixing and long-lasting immunity.

(c) With 40% of transmission occurring before symptoms, the latent period is shorter than the incubation period. Isolating people once they have symptoms can prevent at most 60% of transmission, and in practice much less because of delays. This alone would not bring R below 1. Contacts must be found and quarantined, or tested, quickly, ideally before they become infectious, so speed of testing and tracing is critical.

That 15% of cases cause 80% of transmission indicates strong overdispersion (a low dispersion parameter k), similar to SARS. Most cases infect no one, so many introductions die out by chance, but superspreading events drive growth. Targeting the settings where these events happen, such as crowded, poorly ventilated indoor gatherings, care homes and some workplaces, gives a large effect for proportionate restrictions. Under overdispersion, backward tracing is especially efficient: a case was more likely infected at a cluster event, so finding that source identifies many other infected people. Forward tracing remains necessary to interrupt onward chains.

(d) Early estimates are fragile. Case counts reflect testing as well as infection; if testing expands, the doubling time is underestimated and R overestimated. Reporting delays and changing case definitions distort trends. The serial interval is not the generation interval: with pre-symptomatic transmission it can be shorter or even negative, and early tracing data are right-censored towards short intervals, biasing R downward. Detected clusters are biased towards large or unusual events, and the two approximations show the answer depends on model assumptions. Estimates should carry uncertainty intervals, be checked against admissions, deaths and serosurveys, and be revised often, so early policy should be precautionary and adaptable.

questions.q: According to Parsons' (1951) model of the sick role, which of the following is an OBLIGATION of the sick person?
options: To be exempt from normal social responsibilities
To seek technically competent help and cooperate with it
Not to be held responsible for their illness
To decide alone whether medical treatment is needed
questions.why: Parsons described two rights (exemption from normal duties, not being blamed) and two obligations (wanting to get well, and seeking and cooperating with competent help).

questions.q: In Scambler and Hopkins' study of people with epilepsy, which finding best describes 'felt stigma'?
options: Being refused employment after disclosing the diagnosis
Being labelled by doctors with a diagnosis
Shame and fear of discrimination that led people to conceal their condition, often causing more disruption than actual discrimination
Legal restrictions such as driving bans
questions.why: Felt stigma is the internalised shame and fear of enacted stigma (actual discrimination). Scambler and Hopkins found it was often more disruptive than enacted stigma, because it led to concealment and withdrawal.

questions.q: A GP is consulted by a 46-year-old with three days of sore throat, mild fever and no cough, who says 'I always need antibiotics for this.' Which approach is best supported by evidence for reducing unnecessary antibiotic use while maintaining patient satisfaction?
options: Prescribe immediately, because refusing damages the doctor-patient relationship
Refuse firmly and tell the patient that antibiotics cause resistance
Order a throat swab and prescribe only after the result is back in five days
Explore the patient's concerns, explain the natural course of the illness, use a symptom score, safety-net, and consider a back-up (delayed) prescription
questions.why: Shared decision-making that addresses concerns and expectations, with clear explanation, safety-netting and back-up prescribing where appropriate, reduces antibiotic use without lowering satisfaction. Simply refusing or giving a lecture tends to backfire.

questions.q: Define stigma and give three ways in which stigma can harm the health of people with an infectious disease such as HIV or TB.
markScheme: Definition: an attribute that is deeply discrediting and reduces the person to a 'spoiled identity' (Goffman), involving labelling, stereotyping and discrimination
Delays testing and presentation, so diagnosis is late and transmission continues
Reduces disclosure, engagement with care and adherence to treatment; also causes isolation, anxiety and depression
questions.modelAnswer: Goffman described stigma as a deeply discrediting attribute that reduces a person to a 'spoiled identity'. Others are labelled, stereotyped and discriminated against because of it. In infectious disease, fear of being identified as having HIV or TB may stop people from getting tested, so they are diagnosed late, become more unwell and may unknowingly infect others. Stigma also discourages disclosure to partners, family and employers, which makes it harder to attend appointments or take medication openly, so adherence falls. Finally, both actual and anticipated discrimination cause shame, social isolation, anxiety and depression, which further reduce quality of life and engagement with care.

questions.q: Using the Health Belief Model, explain why a healthy 30-year-old might decline a seasonal influenza vaccine, and suggest how a health campaign could address each factor.
markScheme: Low perceived susceptibility (healthy, young): use messages about personal and household risk and about protecting vulnerable relatives
Low perceived severity ('just flu'): give accurate information about complications and time lost from work
Perceived barriers outweigh benefits (time, cost, fear of side effects, myths such as 'the vaccine gives you flu'): offer convenient workplace or pharmacy vaccination and correct misconceptions
Lack of cues to action and self-efficacy: reminders, invitations, recommendation from a trusted clinician, making booking easy
questions.modelAnswer: The Health Belief Model suggests that behaviour depends on how individuals perceive threat and how they weigh benefits against barriers. A healthy 30-year-old may see their susceptibility as low; a campaign can stress that anyone can catch flu and that vaccination protects babies or elderly relatives. They may see influenza as mild; accurate, non-alarmist information about complications and lost work can correct this. Barriers such as time, inconvenience and myths (for example, that an inactivated vaccine can cause flu) can be reduced by offering vaccination at work or in pharmacies and addressing myths directly. Finally, cues to action, such as text reminders or a personal recommendation from a GP, prompt people to act.

questions.q: A 72-year-old inpatient with MRSA colonisation has been in a single side-room under contact precautions for two weeks. Nurses notice she has become withdrawn, is eating poorly and says 'people treat me like I'm dirty'. Discuss the possible psychological and safety consequences of isolation for this patient, and how the team should balance infection control against her wellbeing.
markScheme: Recognises psychological harms: low mood, anxiety, loneliness, feeling stigmatised or 'dirty', confusion or delirium risk in older people

Recognises safety harms: evidence that isolated patients receive fewer clinician visits and less documented monitoring, and have more preventable adverse events (e.g. Stelfox et al., 2003), such as falls and missed care
Isolation should be justified by risk assessment (organism, site, risk to others, local policy), reviewed regularly and stopped when no longer needed
Practical support: explanation of why precautions are used, encouraging visitors with appropriate precautions, regular check-ins, activities or a phone or tablet
Screen and manage depression or delirium; involve the patient in decisions; staff should avoid stigmatising language and unnecessary personal protective equipment
Balance: the duty to protect other vulnerable patients against the duty of care and the patient's dignity and autonomy; proportionality
questions.modelAnswer: Prolonged isolation can cause low mood, anxiety and loneliness, and visible gloves and gowns can make patients feel contaminated, as her comment shows. Older patients also risk delirium and deconditioning. Isolated patients see clinicians less often and have more preventable adverse events, such as falls and missed observations. Her isolation should be justified and reviewed: does her colonisation pose a real risk to others, and does local policy require a side-room? Precautions should be explained, visitors encouraged with hand hygiene, staff should check in regularly, and her mood should be screened and treated. The team must weigh protecting other patients against her dignity, using the least restrictive effective measures.

questions.q:
Daniel, a 26-year-old graduate trainee, attends a sexual health clinic after a routine screen shows he is HIV-positive. His CD4 count is 540 cells/microlitre and his viral load is 85,000 copies/mL. He is shocked and tearful. He says he has a long-term male partner who he believes is HIV-negative, and adds: 'I can't tell him, and nobody at work or at home can ever find out. My dad would disown me.'

Discuss the psychological and social challenges Daniel faces, and how the clinical team should support him. Include the communication approach, the issue of partner notification and confidentiality, and the role of treatment in his wellbeing and in reducing transmission.
markScheme: Recognises the emotional response to diagnosis: shock, fear, grief, shame, anxiety about the future; risk of depression; offers psychological support and peer support
Uses a structured, empathic communication approach (e.g. SPIKES): exploring understanding, giving information in manageable amounts, responding to emotion
Identifies felt (anticipated) stigma and the risk of enacted stigma from family, intersecting with sexuality and culture; his fear of disownment
Explains that early ART is recommended for all and that with a sustained undetectable viral load he cannot transmit HIV sexually (U = U, PARTNER studies), and that life expectancy is near normal
Partner at current risk (high viral load): discusses condoms and the partner's access to PEP/PrEP and testing; partner notification options (patient referral, provider referral, anonymous)

Confidentiality is central to trust; GMC guidance allows disclosure to a known sexual partner at serious risk if the patient refuses after support, ideally with the patient informed beforehand, and only the minimum necessary
Reassures that disclosure to an employer is not required in general and that HIV is protected as a disability under the Equality Act 2010 from diagnosis
Arranges follow-up, adherence support and links to support organisations
Balances autonomy, beneficence and harm prevention, and reaches a reasoned plan
questions.modelAnswer:
A new HIV diagnosis is often experienced as a crisis. Daniel is likely to feel shock, fear for his health and relationship, guilt about possible transmission and shame shaped by stigma. His fear of being disowned shows felt stigma, made worse by family attitudes towards his sexuality. These reactions can lead to depression, withdrawal or disengagement, so they need to be addressed alongside his physical health.

Communication should be unhurried, private and empathic. Using a framework such as SPIKES, the clinician should explore what Daniel understands, give information in manageable amounts and respond to his distress before moving on to plans. Key messages need to correct outdated beliefs: HIV is now a manageable long-term condition, treatment is recommended for everyone soon after diagnosis, and with effective therapy people have a life expectancy close to normal. Once his viral load is sustained at undetectable levels he will not pass HIV on through sex (U = U, supported by the PARTNER studies). This can reduce shame and give a strong reason to adhere to treatment. Health advisers, psychology services and peer-support organisations can help.

Partner notification is the most delicate issue. With a viral load of 85,000 his partner is at real risk now, and may already be infected. The team should explain why notification matters, both to protect the partner and so the partner can get tested and treated early, and offer options: telling him himself, with coaching, or provider referral. In the meantime the partner should use condoms and have access to post-exposure prophylaxis or PrEP and testing. Confidentiality underpins Daniel's trust and future engagement, and most patients agree to notification with time and support. GMC guidance allows disclosure to a known sexual partner at risk of serious harm if the patient still refuses, ideally after telling the patient and disclosing only what is necessary. This should be a last resort after senior discussion.

Daniel can be reassured that he generally has no obligation to tell his employer, and that HIV is a protected disability under the Equality Act 2010 from the point of diagnosis. Regular follow-up, adherence support and attention to his mental health will help him stay engaged.

questions.q:
Marek, a 41-year-old man, has been sleeping rough in London for two years and drinks alcohol heavily. He presents with three months of cough, night sweats and weight loss, and is diagnosed with smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis that is sensitive to first-line drugs. He leaves hospital against medical advice after four days, saying the ward 'felt like prison'. Over the following month he misses most outpatient appointments.

Analyse the social determinants that contributed to Marek's disease and that now threaten his treatment, using relevant theories or concepts. Propose an evidence-informed, patient-centred plan to support completion of treatment and to protect public health, and discuss the ethical tensions involved.
markScheme: Social determinants: homelessness, overcrowded hostels and night shelters, poverty, malnutrition, alcohol misuse, possible migration from a higher-incidence country, all increasing exposure, reactivation and delays
Barriers to care: competing priorities (food, shelter), distrust of services, previous negative experiences, chaotic lifestyle, transport costs; inverse care law (Tudor Hart)
Psychological factors: stigma of TB and homelessness, fear of confinement, illness perceptions (Leventhal), low self-efficacy
Consequences of poor adherence: treatment failure, relapse, onward transmission, acquired drug resistance (e.g. MDR-TB)
Enhanced case management: a named TB nurse or key worker, directly or video observed therapy, outreach services (e.g. Find&Treat in London), flexible appointments
Address social needs: housing support (TB is a priority for accommodation), food, benefits, alcohol services, peer advocates; incentives or enablers
Contact tracing in shelters; screening with mobile X-ray outreach

Ethical tensions: autonomy and liberty vs public protection; compulsory detention under the Public Health (Control of Disease) Act 1984 (Part 2A orders) only as a proportionate last resort; least restrictive alternative
Building trust and a non-judgemental approach; communication about why the treatment course is long
Coherent analysis linking theory to the plan
questions.modelAnswer:
Marek's TB reflects the social gradient of the disease. In England, TB is concentrated among people experiencing homelessness, people in prison, people who use drugs or alcohol, and migrants from high-incidence countries. Sleeping rough and using crowded night shelters exposes people to infectious cases. Malnutrition and alcohol misuse weaken cell-mediated immunity, increasing the risk of progression and reactivation. Competing survival needs and difficulty accessing primary care delay diagnosis, so he presented after three months, smear-positive and infectious. This illustrates Tudor Hart's inverse care law: those most at risk have the least access to care.

The same factors threaten treatment. TB treatment lasts at least six months, and once symptoms improve its benefit is invisible. Using Leventhal's common-sense model, Marek may see TB as an acute illness that ends when the cough settles. Low self-efficacy, alcohol dependence, the stigma attached to both TB and homelessness, and distrust of institutions all push him away from services, and his description of the ward as 'prison' suggests he fears being controlled. Incomplete treatment risks relapse, ongoing transmission and acquired resistance, which would make treatment much longer, more toxic and more expensive.

A patient-centred plan uses enhanced case management. A named TB nurse or key worker should build a relationship with him. Directly observed therapy can be delivered where he is, through outreach, or by video observed therapy if he has a phone, which avoids repeated clinic visits. London's Find&Treat outreach team and peer advocates with lived experience of TB or homelessness can help engage him. Social needs must be treated as part of care: urgent referral for accommodation, food support, help with benefits, and alcohol services, perhaps alongside small practical enablers such as travel vouchers. Contacts in shelters should be traced and screened, for example with mobile chest X-ray outreach.

The ethical tension is between Marek's autonomy and liberty and protecting others from an airborne infection. Under the Public Health (Control of Disease) Act 1984 a magistrate can make Part 2A orders, including detention in hospital. These should be used only as a last resort when voluntary measures have failed and the risk is significant, following the principles of proportionality and the least restrictive alternative. Coercion can destroy trust and drive people away from services, so a non-judgemental approach that supports him and addresses his social needs is usually both more ethical and more effective.

questions.q:
A GP practice in a deprived area of a large English city audits childhood immunisation. Of 400 children due their first MMR dose by age 2, 300 received it (75%). Among children of parents who attended a practice-run information session, uptake was 54 out of 60. Practice staff record the main reasons given by parents who declined: worries about safety and autism (40%), difficulty getting appointments around work or caring (35%), feeling their child was 'not at risk because measles has gone' (15%), and other reasons (10%).

(a) Calculate MMR uptake among children whose parents did and did not attend a session, and comment on whether the session caused the difference. (b) Using the 3Cs model of vaccine hesitancy, analyse the reasons given. (c) Propose a multi-level strategy to improve uptake, and discuss the ethics of mandatory vaccination policies.
markScheme: Attended: 54/60 = 90%; did not attend: 246/340, about 72.4%
Association, not causation: self-selection (more engaged parents attend), confounding by socioeconomic or other factors; a fair evaluation would need a controlled or randomised design
Confidence: safety and autism concerns rooted in the discredited, retracted 1998 Wakefield paper and misinformation online
Complacency: low perceived risk because the disease is rarely seen, the 'victim of its own success' paradox
Convenience: access barriers, which are partly structural rather than attitudinal; links to the inverse care law and deprivation
Interventions: reminders and recall, flexible and outreach clinics, opportunistic vaccination, home visits for those who face barriers
Communication: trusted clinicians and community leaders, presumptive and motivational interviewing approaches, culturally tailored materials; avoid stigmatising hesitant parents

Mandatory policies: may raise coverage (some countries require vaccination for school entry) but raise concerns about autonomy, may entrench distrust and are not UK policy; consider proportionality and least restrictive means
Notes the need to monitor uptake by subgroup (clustering) and to evaluate interventions
Well-reasoned, structured answer
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Attended: 54/60 = 90%. Did not attend: (300 - 54) / (400 - 60) = 246/340, about 72.4%. Uptake was about 18 percentage points higher among children whose parents attended. This does not show the session caused the improvement. Parents who choose to attend are probably more engaged with health services, may have more flexible jobs, and may already intend to vaccinate (self-selection). Confounding by deprivation, language or family structure is likely. A fair test would need comparison groups, ideally randomised (for example, randomising invitations), with adjustment for baseline differences.

(b) The 3Cs model separates confidence, complacency and convenience. Concerns about safety and autism (40%) reflect low confidence. They can be traced to Wakefield's 1998 paper, which was retracted in 2010 and has been refuted by large studies, but the claims still circulate online and in some communities. The belief that 'measles has gone' (15%) reflects complacency: successful vaccination makes the disease invisible, so the perceived risk falls. Appointment difficulties (35%) relate to convenience, a structural barrier that is especially relevant in a deprived area where parents may work irregular hours or lack childcare. A large share of non-vaccination therefore reflects access rather than opposition, which practices can change directly.

(c) A multi-level strategy should match each cause. For convenience: automated reminders and active recall, evening and weekend clinics, drop-in sessions, opportunistic vaccination at any contact, and outreach or home visits through health visitors. For confidence: brief, respectful conversations with a trusted clinician, using a presumptive approach and motivational interviewing for hesitant parents; acknowledging concerns rather than dismissing them; and working with community and faith leaders and translated materials. For complacency: explaining recent measles outbreaks and complications in local, relatable terms. Uptake should be monitored by subgroup, because clusters of unvaccinated children drive outbreaks, and the effect of each intervention should be evaluated.

Mandatory vaccination, such as requiring vaccination for school or nursery entry as some countries do, can raise coverage but restricts parental autonomy, may penalise families who face access barriers rather than refusing, and can harden distrust among hesitant parents. The UK relies on voluntary vaccination. Ethically, coercion is justified only if less restrictive measures have failed and the public health risk is serious. Removing barriers and building trust should come first.

questions.q:
'Public health measures such as quarantine and isolation inevitably trade individual wellbeing for collective benefit.'

Critically evaluate this statement, drawing on evidence about the psychological and social effects of quarantine and isolation (in hospital and in the community) and on ethical and legal frameworks for controlling infectious disease in the UK.
markScheme: Defines quarantine (separating exposed, well people) vs isolation (separating infected people)

Evidence of individual harm: Brooks et al. (2020) review of quarantine (post-traumatic stress symptoms, anger, confusion; stressors such as duration, fear, boredom, inadequate supplies and information, financial loss)
Hospital isolation: fewer clinician visits and more adverse events, anxiety and depression, stigma
Harms are unequally distributed: people in insecure work, crowded housing, with existing mental illness or living alone; financial loss and inequalities

Counterpoint: harms are not inevitable; they can be reduced by short duration, clear rationale and communication, practical and financial support (e.g. sick pay), voluntary framing and altruistic framing
Counterpoint: individuals also benefit, by protecting their families, gaining earlier diagnosis and treatment, and from reduced epidemic burden; the 'trade-off' framing is too simple
Ethical frameworks: Mill's harm principle; proportionality, necessity, least restrictive alternative, reciprocity (society's duty to support those restricted), transparency; Siracusa Principles

UK legal frameworks: Public Health (Control of Disease) Act 1984 and Part 2A orders; Human Rights Act 1998 (Article 5 right to liberty with exception for preventing spread of infectious disease, Article 8); Coronavirus Act 2020 as a time-limited emergency measure
Evaluation of effectiveness: benefit depends on pathogen characteristics (e.g. pre-symptomatic transmission), adherence and timing; ineffective measures cannot justify their harms
Reasoned conclusion and sophisticated structure
questions.modelAnswer:
Isolation separates people known to be infected; quarantine restricts healthy people who have been exposed. The statement captures a real tension but overstates it: the harms are real, but neither inevitable nor simply traded for collective benefit.

The evidence of harm is substantial. Brooks and colleagues' 2020 rapid review found frequent post-traumatic stress symptoms, confusion and anger, worsened by longer quarantine, fear of infection, boredom, inadequate supplies and information, and financial loss. Patients under hospital contact isolation receive fewer clinician visits, have been reported to experience more preventable adverse events, and report more anxiety, depression and stigma. The burden falls hardest on people in insecure work without sick pay, in overcrowded housing, living alone or with existing mental illness, which widens inequalities and, by reducing adherence, also reduces collective benefit.

However, 'inevitably' does not hold. The same review identified what reduces harm: keeping quarantine short, explaining why it is needed, providing supplies and financial support, and framing compliance as voluntary and altruistic. The principle of reciprocity holds that society owes support to those it restricts. Hospital isolation can be reviewed often and ended when unnecessary. The trade-off framing also ignores benefits to the individual: protecting their own household, earlier diagnosis and treatment, and living in a community where epidemics are controlled.

Ethical frameworks also limit any trade-off. Mill's harm principle allows liberty to be restricted to prevent harm to others, and public health ethics adds necessity, proportionality, effectiveness, the least restrictive alternative and transparency, as reflected in the Siracusa Principles. In UK law, the Public Health (Control of Disease) Act 1984 allows magistrates to impose restrictions through Part 2A orders only where there is a significant risk and on the basis of evidence. The Human Rights Act 1998 incorporates Article 5 of the ECHR, which permits lawful detention to prevent the spread of infectious disease, while proportionality is still required. The Coronavirus Act 2020 was time-limited and subject to parliamentary renewal, which reflects concern about emergency powers.

Finally, the strength of the collective benefit is itself an empirical question. Symptom-based isolation is less effective against pathogens with substantial pre-symptomatic transmission, and measures that are poorly followed or applied late impose costs with little gain. The statement is therefore best revised: quarantine and isolation impose real individual costs, but these can and should be minimised and compensated, and are justified only when the measures actually work.

questions.q: Which antibiotic class acts by inhibiting bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV?
options: Fluoroquinolones
Macrolides
Aminoglycosides
Glycopeptides
questions.why: Fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin trap gyrase and topoisomerase IV on DNA, causing double-strand breaks. Macrolides and aminoglycosides inhibit protein synthesis, and glycopeptides block cell wall synthesis.

questions.q: A Klebsiella pneumoniae isolate from a urinary catheter is resistant to ceftriaxone and ceftazidime, but susceptible to meropenem. Its resistance is lost when clavulanic acid is added. What is the most likely mechanism?
options: Production of PBP2a encoded by mecA
An extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)
A metallo-carbapenemase such as NDM
Alteration of D-Ala-D-Ala to D-Ala-D-Lac
questions.why: ESBLs hydrolyse third-generation cephalosporins, are inhibited by clavulanate and usually spare carbapenems. Metallo-carbapenemases hydrolyse carbapenems and are not inhibited by clavulanate. PBP2a and D-Ala-D-Lac are Gram-positive mechanisms (MRSA and VRE).

questions.q: A patient with a severe Gram-negative infection is to be treated with an aminoglycoside. Which statement about its pharmacodynamics is correct?
options: Killing depends mainly on the time the drug concentration stays above the MIC, so continuous infusion is preferred
It is bacteriostatic, so it should be combined with a bactericidal drug
Killing is concentration-dependent (Cmax/MIC) with a post-antibiotic effect, which supports once-daily high-peak regimens
It is highly active against anaerobes because uptake is independent of oxygen
questions.why: Aminoglycosides kill in a concentration-dependent way and have a significant post-antibiotic effect, which supports high-peak, extended-interval dosing. Their uptake needs oxygen-dependent transport, so anaerobes are intrinsically resistant.

questions.q: Explain the principle of selective toxicity and give two examples of antibacterial targets that make it possible.
markScheme: Selective toxicity: the drug harms the microbe at concentrations that do little harm to the host, by acting on targets that are absent or different in human cells
Example 1: peptidoglycan cell wall synthesis (beta-lactams, glycopeptides), which human cells lack

Example 2: bacterial 70S ribosomes (aminoglycosides, macrolides, tetracyclines), DNA gyrase (fluoroquinolones) or bacterial folate synthesis (sulfonamides, which work because humans take in folate from the diet)
questions.modelAnswer: Selective toxicity means an antimicrobial damages the pathogen at concentrations that are tolerated by the patient. It works best when the drug's target is absent from human cells or differs substantially from the human version. Peptidoglycan, the target of beta-lactams and glycopeptides, exists only in bacteria. Bacterial 70S ribosomes, targeted by aminoglycosides and macrolides, differ structurally from human 80S cytoplasmic ribosomes. Sulfonamides block bacterial folate synthesis, whereas humans obtain folate from food. Selectivity is never absolute; mitochondrial ribosomes resemble bacterial ones, which helps explain some aminoglycoside and linezolid toxicity.

questions.q: Describe four general mechanisms by which bacteria can become resistant to antibiotics, giving an example of each.
markScheme: Enzymatic inactivation, e.g. beta-lactamases (including ESBLs and carbapenemases) or aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes
Target alteration, e.g. PBP2a in MRSA, D-Ala-D-Lac in VRE, rpoB mutations (rifampicin) or gyrA mutations (fluoroquinolones)
Reduced permeability, e.g. loss of outer membrane porins in Gram-negatives (e.g. carbapenem resistance in Pseudomonas with OprD loss)
Efflux pumps, e.g. tetracycline efflux or multidrug pumps such as AcrAB-TolC in Enterobacterales (credit target bypass, e.g. alternative DHFR for trimethoprim)
questions.modelAnswer: Bacteria can destroy or modify the drug: beta-lactamases hydrolyse the beta-lactam ring, and some enzymes add chemical groups that inactivate aminoglycosides. They can change the target: MRSA makes PBP2a, which beta-lactams bind poorly; enterococci change their peptidoglycan precursor to D-Ala-D-Lac to escape vancomycin; and mutations in rpoB or gyrA reduce binding of rifampicin or fluoroquinolones. Gram-negatives can reduce entry by losing porins, for example Pseudomonas losing OprD and becoming less susceptible to carbapenems. Efflux pumps actively expel drugs, from tetracycline-specific pumps to multidrug systems such as AcrAB-TolC. These genes often spread on plasmids and transposons.

questions.q: Using knowledge of drug mechanisms and resistance, explain why active pulmonary tuberculosis is treated with a combination of drugs for at least six months. Assume that spontaneous resistance mutations occur in about 1 in 10^6 bacilli for isoniazid and 1 in 10^8 for rifampicin, and that a cavity may contain around 10^8-10^9 bacilli.
markScheme: Mechanisms: isoniazid is a prodrug activated by KatG that inhibits mycolic acid synthesis (InhA); rifampicin inhibits RNA polymerase (rpoB); pyrazinamide is activated by PncA and acts on slowly metabolising bacilli in acidic conditions; ethambutol inhibits arabinosyl transferases (arabinogalactan)
With 10^8-10^9 bacilli, resistant mutants to any single drug are almost certainly already present, so monotherapy selects resistance
Resistance mutations are independent, so the chance of a bacillus resisting both is about 10^-6 x 10^-8 = 10^-14, which is far fewer than one bacillus in the cavity

Slow growth and populations in different metabolic states (active vs semi-dormant, extracellular vs intracellular in acidic phagosomes) require prolonged treatment, with rifampicin and pyrazinamide sterilising persisters
Intensive phase (four drugs) reduces bacterial load quickly; continuation phase (isoniazid plus rifampicin) eliminates persisters and prevents relapse

Poor adherence leads to effective monotherapy, acquired resistance (MDR-TB = resistant to isoniazid and rifampicin) and relapse, hence directly observed therapy or enhanced case management when needed
questions.modelAnswer: Isoniazid is activated by mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase (KatG) and inhibits InhA, blocking mycolic acid synthesis. Rifampicin inhibits RNA polymerase. Pyrazinamide, activated by PncA, kills semi-dormant bacilli in acidic environments, and ethambutol blocks arabinogalactan synthesis. A cavity with 10^8-10^9 bacilli will already contain hundreds of isoniazid-resistant mutants and probably some rifampicin-resistant ones, so a single drug would select them. Because mutations are independent, resistance to both drugs occurs at about 10^-14, which is effectively never. Mycobacteria divide slowly and include semi-dormant persisters, so an intensive phase of four drugs is followed by a continuation phase of rifampicin and isoniazid to sterilise lesions and prevent relapse. Missed doses can lead to MDR-TB.

questions.q:
A 78-year-old care-home resident is treated with co-amoxiclav for a chest infection, and then with ciprofloxacin for a urinary tract infection. She is also taking a proton pump inhibitor. Ten days later she develops profuse watery diarrhoea (seven episodes a day), abdominal pain and fever of 38.4 C. Her white cell count is 19 x 10^9/L and creatinine has risen from 80 to 140 micromol/L. A stool test is positive for Clostridioides difficile glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) and toxin.

Explain how antibiotic exposure led to this infection, interpret the investigations, outline the principles of management in terms of drug classes and mechanisms, and describe the infection prevention and antimicrobial stewardship measures that follow.
markScheme: Broad-spectrum antibiotics (co-amoxiclav, fluoroquinolone) disrupt the colonic microbiota, removing colonisation resistance (including secondary bile acid metabolism that normally inhibits spore germination)

Spores, ingested from the environment or already carried, germinate; vegetative cells produce toxins A and B (TcdA, TcdB), which glucosylate Rho GTPases, disrupting the cytoskeleton and tight junctions and causing inflammation and pseudomembranous colitis
Additional risk factors: older age, care-home residence, PPI use, comorbidity
Two-stage testing: GDH shows the organism is present; toxin positivity indicates active toxin-mediated disease rather than colonisation
Severity markers: WCC above 15 x 10^9/L and rising creatinine indicate severe CDI

Management: stop unnecessary antibiotics and PPI review; fluids; avoid antimotility drugs; oral glycopeptide (vancomycin) or fidaxomicin (macrocyclic RNA polymerase inhibitor, narrow spectrum and lower recurrence) acting in the gut lumen
Escalation if complicated (ileus, toxic megacolon): surgical review; recurrences may need faecal microbiota transplant
Infection prevention: isolation in a side room with its own toilet, gloves and aprons, soap-and-water handwashing (alcohol gel does not kill spores), sporicidal (chlorine) cleaning
Surveillance and reporting (mandatory reporting of C. difficile cases in England), root cause analysis
Stewardship: avoid high-risk antibiotics where possible, review at 48-72 hours (Start Smart - Then Focus), use the shortest effective course
questions.modelAnswer:
C. difficile is an anaerobic, spore-forming, Gram-positive bacillus. Normally the diverse colonic microbiota resists colonisation by competing for nutrients and by converting primary bile acids, which promote spore germination, into secondary bile acids, which inhibit vegetative growth. Co-amoxiclav and ciprofloxacin are broad-spectrum and among the antibiotics most strongly linked to C. difficile infection. They disrupt this ecosystem, allowing spores swallowed from the care-home environment, or already present, to germinate and multiply. Toxigenic strains produce toxins A and B, which glucosylate Rho-family GTPases in colonocytes. This collapses the actin cytoskeleton, opens tight junctions and triggers neutrophil-rich inflammation, causing watery diarrhoea and, in severe cases, pseudomembranous colitis. Older age, care-home residence and PPI use add to her risk.

In UK practice, testing is done in two stages. GDH shows the organism is present, and a positive toxin test indicates active toxin production, so this is infection rather than colonisation. A white cell count above 15 x 10^9/L and acute kidney injury mark this as a severe episode.

Management starts with stopping unnecessary antibiotics where possible and reviewing the PPI, giving fluid and electrolyte replacement, and avoiding antimotility drugs, which can precipitate toxic megacolon. Specific treatment uses oral agents that act within the gut lumen. Oral vancomycin, a glycopeptide that inhibits cell wall synthesis, is poorly absorbed and so reaches high concentrations in the colon. Fidaxomicin is a macrocyclic antibiotic that inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase with a narrow spectrum, which spares more of the normal flora and is associated with fewer recurrences. Signs of ileus, colonic dilatation or worsening sepsis require senior and surgical review. Repeated recurrences may be treated with faecal microbiota transplantation, which restores colonisation resistance.

Infection prevention: she should be isolated in a single room with her own toilet. Staff should wear gloves and aprons and wash hands with soap and water, because alcohol does not kill spores. The environment needs chlorine-based sporicidal cleaning. Cases are reported for mandatory surveillance in England, and a root cause analysis examines whether the antibiotic courses were appropriate. Stewardship lessons include preferring narrower agents where guidelines allow, reviewing therapy at 48-72 hours under Start Smart - Then Focus, using the shortest effective courses and regularly auditing prescribing in care homes.

questions.q:
A 64-year-old man with a prosthetic aortic valve presents with fever and a new murmur. Three sets of blood cultures grow Enterococcus faecalis. Laboratory results: ampicillin MIC 1 mg/L (susceptible), vancomycin susceptible, and no high-level gentamicin resistance. Two weeks into treatment, a second patient on the same cardiac ward has bacteraemia with Enterococcus faecium that is resistant to ampicillin and vancomycin (VRE).

(a) Explain why bactericidal combination therapy is used for enterococcal endocarditis, describing the mechanisms of the drug classes involved and the basis of synergy. (b) Explain why biofilm on prosthetic material makes this infection harder to cure. (c) Explain the molecular basis of vancomycin resistance in the second patient's isolate, how it spreads, and the drug classes that remain active, with their mechanisms. (d) Outline the infection prevention response on the ward.
markScheme: Endocarditis vegetations are dense, poorly vascularised and contain slowly growing bacteria protected from phagocytes, so bactericidal therapy is required
Beta-lactams (ampicillin) bind PBPs and block peptidoglycan cross-linking; alone they are mainly bacteriostatic against enterococci
Aminoglycosides bind the 30S subunit, causing mistranslation; enterococci are intrinsically resistant to low concentrations because of poor uptake

Synergy: wall damage from the beta-lactam increases aminoglycoside uptake, giving bactericidal killing; lost if there is high-level aminoglycoside resistance; alternative ampicillin plus ceftriaxone (saturation of complementary PBPs) avoids nephrotoxicity
Biofilm: extracellular matrix, slow-growing and persister cells, poor drug penetration and immune evasion; prosthetic valve infection often needs surgery and prolonged therapy
VRE: vanA (or vanB) gene clusters on transposons such as Tn1546, often plasmid-borne, change the terminal D-Ala-D-Ala to D-Ala-D-Lac, reducing vancomycin binding about 1000-fold
Spread: horizontal gene transfer and clonal spread; selection by broad-spectrum antibiotics; gut colonisation and environmental persistence; hospital transmission on hands and equipment
Remaining options: linezolid (50S, 23S rRNA, blocks initiation complex) and daptomycin (calcium-dependent membrane depolarisation); possibly tigecycline (30S glycylcycline); microbiology advice
IPC: contact precautions and isolation or cohorting, hand hygiene, enhanced environmental cleaning, screening of contacts, typing to look for transmission, stewardship review
Organised, mechanism-focused answer with evaluation
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Endocarditis vegetations are dense masses of platelets and fibrin in which bacteria reach very high numbers, often grow slowly and are shielded from phagocytes. Host defences cannot reliably clear organisms that are merely inhibited, so bactericidal therapy is needed. Ampicillin, a beta-lactam, binds penicillin-binding proteins and stops peptidoglycan cross-linking. Against enterococci it is mainly bacteriostatic, partly because their PBPs have low affinity. Aminoglycosides such as gentamicin bind the 30S ribosomal subunit and cause mistranslation, but enterococci are intrinsically resistant to clinically achievable concentrations because the drug enters poorly. When given together, damage to the wall from the beta-lactam increases aminoglycoside entry, producing synergistic bactericidal killing. This only works if the isolate lacks high-level aminoglycoside resistance, so the laboratory tests specifically for it. Because aminoglycosides are nephrotoxic and ototoxic, especially in older patients over long courses, ampicillin plus ceftriaxone is a widely used alternative for E. faecalis: the two beta-lactams saturate complementary PBPs and together kill the organism.

(b) On prosthetic material, enterococci form biofilms, communities embedded in an extracellular matrix.
