Drugs penetrate the matrix slowly, many cells are metabolically inactive persisters that beta-lactams kill poorly, and phagocytes cannot engulf the biofilm. Prosthetic valve endocarditis therefore needs prolonged combination therapy and often surgical valve replacement.

(c) Vancomycin binds the D-Ala-D-Ala end of peptidoglycan precursors. VRE carrying the vanA cluster, usually on transposon Tn1546 within a transferable plasmid, make precursors ending in D-Ala-D-Lac instead and destroy the normal D-Ala-D-Ala precursors. Vancomycin binds the modified target about 1000-fold less strongly. vanB works similarly. These genes spread both horizontally and through successful hospital clones of E. faecium, which colonise the gut of patients given broad-spectrum antibiotics, persist on surfaces and are carried on hands. Ampicillin resistance in E. faecium reflects altered PBP5. Remaining options, chosen with microbiology advice, include linezolid, which binds 23S rRNA on the 50S subunit and prevents formation of the initiation complex, and daptomycin, a lipopeptide that inserts into the membrane in a calcium-dependent way and depolarises it.

(d) Two patients with enterococcal infection on the same ward warrant investigation, although different species suggest they are not linked. The VRE patient should be isolated with contact precautions. Hand hygiene and enhanced environmental cleaning are needed, and contacts should be screened for VRE colonisation. Isolates should be typed to look for transmission, and ward prescribing reviewed, because cephalosporin and glycopeptide use select for VRE.

questions.q:
A hospital antimicrobial stewardship team reviews a medical ward over one month. Of 120 patients on antibiotics, only 66 had the indication documented, 48 had a 48-72 hour review recorded, and 30 were still on intravenous therapy despite meeting criteria to switch to oral. Of 40 patients started on piperacillin-tazobactam for presumed sepsis, 28 had cultures taken before the first dose, and in 12 of these 28 a narrower agent was appropriate once results were available, but only 4 were changed.

(a) Calculate the percentages for each measure. (b) Explain, with reference to drug mechanisms and resistance, why unnecessary or prolonged use of broad-spectrum agents such as piperacillin-tazobactam is harmful to the individual and to the hospital population. (c) Propose a stewardship improvement plan, and discuss behavioural factors that influence prescribers.
markScheme: Indication documented 66/120 = 55%; 48-72 h review 48/120 = 40%; eligible but still IV 30/120 = 25% of all patients on antibiotics
Cultures before first dose 28/40 = 70%; de-escalation 4/12 = 33% of patients where it was appropriate
Piperacillin is a ureidopenicillin (binds PBPs); tazobactam is a beta-lactamase inhibitor; broad spectrum including Pseudomonas and anaerobes
Individual harms: C. difficile infection, disruption of the microbiota, colonisation with resistant organisms, adverse drug reactions, line complications from IV therapy

Population harms: selection pressure for ESBL- and carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales and resistant Pseudomonas; increased carbapenem use creates a cycle of escalation; horizontal gene transfer on plasmids

Improvement: Start Smart - Then Focus, prompts in electronic prescribing for indication and review, IV-to-oral switch criteria, stewardship ward rounds, rapid diagnostics, local guidelines, audit and feedback
Behavioural factors: fear of missing sepsis and of litigation, diagnostic uncertainty, hierarchy and reluctance to change seniors' prescriptions, 'prescribing etiquette', habit, time pressure
Behaviour-change approaches: feedback with peer comparison, education, decision support, senior endorsement, making the right choice the easy one
Measuring outcomes: repeat audit (PDSA cycles), C. difficile rates, antibiotic consumption, resistance trends, balancing measures such as sepsis outcomes
Well-organised answer integrating pharmacology and behaviour
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Indication documented: 66/120 = 55%. 48-72 hour review: 48/120 = 40%. Eligible for oral switch but still on IV therapy: 30/120 = 25% of patients on antibiotics. Cultures before piperacillin-tazobactam: 28/40 = 70%. De-escalation when appropriate: 4/12, about 33%. Every measure falls well short of good practice, and the poor culture rate makes later de-escalation harder, because without results clinicians are reluctant to narrow therapy.

(b) Piperacillin is a ureidopenicillin that binds penicillin-binding proteins and blocks peptidoglycan cross-linking. Tazobactam inhibits many beta-lactamases, protecting it. The combination covers Pseudomonas, many Enterobacterales and anaerobes. This breadth is valuable in sepsis but harmful when continued unnecessarily. For the individual, it destroys the anaerobic gut flora, removing colonisation resistance and predisposing to C. difficile and to colonisation with resistant organisms. Adverse reactions are also possible, and unnecessary IV therapy adds line infections, phlebitis and longer stays. For the hospital, sustained use selects for organisms producing ESBLs, AmpC and carbapenemases and for resistant Pseudomonas. Resistance genes on plasmids spread between species and patients. Resistance then pushes prescribers towards carbapenems, which in turn selects for carbapenemase producers, a cycle of escalation that ends with very few treatment options.

(c) The plan should follow Start Smart - Then Focus. Electronic prescribing should require an indication and planned duration, and should trigger a mandatory 48-72 hour review with clear choices: stop, switch IV to oral, narrow, continue or outpatient therapy. Blood cultures should be taken before antibiotics through sepsis bundles. Microbiologists or pharmacists should run regular stewardship rounds, local guidelines should promote narrower first-line choices, IV-to-oral switch criteria should be made visible at the bedside, and rapid diagnostics can speed de-escalation. Prescribing should be audited repeatedly using plan-do-study-act cycles, tracking antibiotic consumption, C. difficile and resistance rates, with sepsis mortality as a balancing measure.

Behaviour is central. Junior doctors face diagnostic uncertainty and fear missing sepsis, so broad-spectrum antibiotics feel safe. 'Prescribing etiquette' and hierarchy make them reluctant to change a senior's choice, and continuing a prescription takes less effort than reviewing it. Effective approaches include audit and feedback with comparison against peers, visible senior endorsement, decision support that makes the right choice the default, and building a ward culture in which stopping or narrowing antibiotics is seen as good care rather than a risk.

questions.q:
'Antimicrobial resistance is an inevitable consequence of Darwinian evolution; the best we can hope for is to slow it down.'

Critically evaluate this statement. Draw on the molecular mechanisms and genetics of resistance, the fitness costs of resistance, human and veterinary antimicrobial use (One Health), and the strategies available to preserve existing drugs and develop new ones.
markScheme: Accepts the core Darwinian logic: variation (mutation, horizontal gene transfer), selection by antimicrobial exposure, heritability; resistance genes pre-date clinical antibiotics (found in ancient permafrost DNA)
Genetics: chromosomal mutation (rpoB, gyrA) vs mobile genetic elements (plasmids, transposons, integrons) carrying multiple resistance genes; co-selection by metals and biocides

Fitness costs: resistance can reduce fitness, so in principle it may decline when use falls; but compensatory mutations and low-cost plasmids limit reversal, so reversibility is often slow or incomplete
Evidence that use drives resistance: correlation between national antibiotic consumption and resistance; emergence of mcr-1 linked to colistin use in agriculture
One Health: agricultural use, environmental contamination (pharmaceutical effluent, sewage), global travel and spread (e.g. NDM)

Strategies to preserve drugs: stewardship, infection prevention (fewer infections, fewer prescriptions), vaccination (e.g. pneumococcal conjugate vaccines reduced resistant strains), diagnostics, combination therapy (TB, HIV)

New approaches: new classes and beta-lactamase inhibitors (e.g. avibactam), phage therapy, antibodies, anti-virulence drugs (less selective pressure), microbiome approaches; economic incentives such as the UK subscription model

Evaluates 'inevitable': resistance to some drugs has remained low or emerged slowly (e.g. penicillin still treats Streptococcus pyogenes; syphilis still penicillin-susceptible), showing that the rate depends on biology and use
Evaluates 'best we can hope for': combining strategies can keep drugs useful indefinitely, and some interventions (vaccines, anti-virulence drugs) reduce the selective pressure itself
Policy context: UK national action plan and WHO Global Action Plan (2015)
Nuanced conclusion and sophisticated argument
questions.modelAnswer:
The statement rests on sound biology. Bacterial populations are huge, reproduce quickly and vary through mutation and horizontal transfer of genes on plasmids, transposons and integrons, so any antimicrobial exposure selects for resistant variants. Resistance genes are ancient: beta-lactamase and vancomycin-resistance genes have been found in permafrost DNA about 30,000 years old, because microbes evolved alongside natural antibiotics. Resistance to any widely used agent is therefore expected.

However, 'inevitable' hides wide variation in how quickly and how much resistance appears. Rifampicin resistance arises from single rpoB mutations within one patient if the drug is given alone, whereas Streptococcus pyogenes remains essentially fully susceptible to penicillin after eight decades, and Treponema pallidum is still treated with penicillin. The difference reflects the drug's target, the organism's biology and how the drug is used. Combination therapy in TB and HIV prevents resistance in individual patients by requiring several independent mutations at once.

Use is the main controllable driver. Countries that consume more antibiotics have more resistance, and plasmid-borne mcr-1 colistin resistance (reported in 2015) emerged amid heavy agricultural colistin use. A One Health view links animal and human use, environmental contamination and global travel, as the worldwide spread of NDM carbapenemases shows.

Fitness costs suggest resistance might decline when use falls, but compensatory mutations, low-cost plasmids and co-selection (one plasmid carrying several resistance genes, or genes for metal and biocide resistance) often keep it stable. Reversal is possible but slow and incomplete.

The second half of the statement is too pessimistic. Several strategies reduce selective pressure rather than just slowing evolution. Vaccines prevent infections and so prescriptions: pneumococcal conjugate vaccines reduced invasive disease, including disease caused by resistant serotypes. Infection prevention and rapid diagnostics reduce unnecessary use. Stewardship under national and WHO action plans limits exposure. Development continues: new beta-lactamase inhibitors such as avibactam have restored activity against some carbapenemase producers, while phage therapy, monoclonal antibodies and anti-virulence drugs that disarm rather than kill may exert weaker selection. The UK's subscription-style payment model for antimicrobials tries to fix the market failure that discourages companies from developing drugs that will be kept in reserve.

Resistance is therefore an evolutionary certainty in principle, but its pace and clinical impact are not fixed. A combined approach of prevention, stewardship, One Health regulation and innovation could keep effective treatment available indefinitely, which is more than simply slowing an unavoidable decline.
